title: How to Pretty-Print Your Kubernetes YAML as KYAML and Why You'd Want To
text:
How to Pretty-Print Your Kubernetes YAML as KYAML and Why You'd Want To
YAML has been the standard way to write Kubernetes manifests for years. Every example, tutorial, and configuration file you come across is written in it. The problem isn't that YAML is a bad format. It's that YAML gives you a lot of choices, and not all of them are equally good for writing Kubernetes manifests. Some features make files harder to read, some are easy to misuse and others can lead to surprising behavior.
The interesting part is that Kubernetes doesn't actually need most of those features. It only relies on a small subset of YAML. This led to a simple question: if Kubernetes only needs a small part of YAML, why not standardize on that part and avoid the rest? Instead of introducing a new configuration language, SIG CLI introduced KYAML, a stricter, more consistent way to write YAML.
What is KYAML?
KYAML is a strict subset (or "dialect") of standard YAML, designed to be parseable by the existing ecosystem without any changes, as proposed in KEP 5295. It does not introduce a new format or a new parser. It just narrows the scope of choices you make when writing YAML, so everyone ends up making the same ones.
Think of it less like a new language and more like an agreed-upon style. Everything valid in KYAML is valid YAML.
How KYAML solves it
Standard YAML has a few well-known traps and JSON is not without its own.
Whitespace sensitivity. Indentation defines structure in YAML, which means a wrongly indented file can remain syntactically valid while representing a different object than intended. This gets especially painful with templating tools like Helm, where you are manipulating indentation from outside the YAML context.
Silent type coercion. String quoting is optional in YAML, which sounds convenient until it is not. Some values that look like strings get coerced into other types without warning. The classic example is the "Norway Bug".
country: NO
In standard YAML, NO is parsed as a boolean false, not the string "NO" and it has caught more than a few people off guard.
JSON is not the answer either. It lacks comment support, is strict about trailing commas, and requires every key to be quoted, none of which makes for a good config writing experience.
KYAML addresses all of these by making structure and types explicit:
- Does not depend on whitespace for structure
- Always quotes value strings so no silent type coercion
- Always uses {} for maps and structs
- Always uses [] for lists
- Allows comments and trailing commas, unlike JSON
- Includes a --- header to distinguish it from JSON at a glance, since both start with {
YAML calls this flow style, as opposed to the conventional block style most people use. KYAML sits halfway between JSON and YAML, more explicit than default YAML, friendlier than JSON.
Here is the same Pod manifest written in both formats for comparison.
Standard YAML
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: my-pod
  labels:
    app: demo
spec:
  containers:
    - name: nginx
      image: nginx:1.20
KYAML
---
{
  apiVersion: "v1",
  kind: "Pod",
  metadata: {
    name: "my-pod",
    labels: {
      app: "demo",
    },
  },
  spec: {
    containers: [{
      name: "nginx",
      image: "nginx:1.20",
    }],
  },
}
Notice the double-quoted string values, the braces around every mapping, the brackets around the list and the trailing commas. The additional syntax makes the document structure explicit instead of relying on indentation.
How to pretty print YAML as KYAML
There are different ways to get KYAML output.
Option 1: kubectl -o kyaml
Since Kubernetes 1.34, kubectl supports KYAML as a native output format.
# Kubernetes 1.35+ (beta; feature enabled by default, still requires -o kyaml CLI param)
kubectl get deployment my-app -o kyaml
# Kubernetes 1.34 (alpha, opt-in)
export KUBECTL_KYAML=true
kubectl get deployment my-app -o kyaml
To save the output to a file:
kubectl get deployment my-app -o kyaml > my-app.yaml
There are currently no plans to make KYAML the default output format. If you prefer using KYAML by default, you can configure your preferred default with kuberc. For more details, see the kuberc documentation.
# Kubernetes 1.36+
kubectl kuberc set --section defaults --command get --option output=kyaml
# Kubernetes 1.33–1.35 (alpha prefix still required)
kubectl alpha kuberc set --section defaults --command get --option output=kyaml
Option 2: Kubernetes' yamlfmt
sigs.k8s.io/yaml ships a yamlfmt tool that can convert files to KYAML.
Install via Go:
go install sigs.k8s.io/yaml/yamlfmt@latest
Running it against a file prints the KYAML version to stdout. It also accepts a directory, in which case it converts and prints every file in that directory. So you'll need to redirect the output to a file (or files) if you want the conversion to stick.
yamlfmt -o=kyaml my-deployment.yaml
It can also show you a diff instead of a full conversion:
yamlfmt -o=kyaml -d my-deployment.yaml
Option 3: Google's yamlfmt
For converting existing files, Google's yamlfmt added a dedicated kyaml formatter in v0.21.0.
Install via Go, or grab a binary from the releases page:
go install github.com/google/yamlfmt/cmd/yamlfmt@latest
It is also available as a pre-commit hook and as a Docker image for CI pipelines.
Add a .yamlfmt config to your project root:
formatter:
  type: kyaml
Preview the output without modifying your file:
yamlfmt -dry my-deployment.yaml
then apply:
yamlfmt my-deployment.yaml
To convert an entire directory:
yamlfmt ./k8s/
The kyaml formatter takes no additional configuration and does not share options with the default formatter so mixing them will cause an error.
For more on the available modes and flags, check the command usage docs.
Is KYAML worth adopting?
Every valid KYAML file is a valid YAML file. So whatever you write in KYAML, your existing tools, your kubectl, your CI pipelines, none of them need to change. You can even pass KYAML as input to any version of kubectl, not just 1.34+, because at the end of the day it is just YAML.
KYAML is not strictly necessary. You can keep writing block-style YAML and things will work. But it is a deliberate choice to make your configs less error-prone and more consistent especially across a team or a larger repo.
It is less of a migration and more of a better habit.

title: Gateway API v1.6: TCPRoute and UDPRoute Graduate to Standard
text:
Gateway API v1.6: TCPRoute and UDPRoute Graduate to Standard
The Kubernetes SIG Network community is thrilled to share the release of Gateway API v1.6.0, which was released on June 30th of this year!
Gateway API has become the standard for modern, role-oriented, and expressive service networking in Kubernetes. In previous releases, Gateway API established a production-grade foundation for HTTP and TLS layer 7 traffic. With version 1.6.0, Gateway API takes a major step forward by expanding standard layer 4 protocol routing and introducing cleaner API boundaries for experimental innovation.
Here is a quick summary of what's new in Gateway API v1.6.0:
- TCPRoute and UDPRoute Graduate to Standard: Raw L4 TCP and UDP traffic routing reach GA stability in the v1 API version.
- Experimental API Group Separation: Experimental resources transition to a distinct API group (gateway.networking.x-k8s.io) with an X prefix to make experimental vs. standard boundaries crystal clear.
Let's dive into the details!
TCPRoute and UDPRoute graduate to Standard
Leads: Nick Young, Ricardo Katz and Zac Nixon
Until now, Gateway API only offered a stable routing model for HTTP and TLS traffic. Workloads that speak a raw protocol over TCP or UDP - databases, DNS, VoIP, gaming, IoT telemetry - had no portable way to plug into a Gateway. Users either fell back to a plain Kubernetes Service, or to an implementation-specific CRD that doesn't travel between Gateway controllers.
TCPRoute and UDPRoute close that gap: they route traffic to backends based on protocol and port alone, no L7 awareness required.
With this release, both have graduated from the Experimental channel to Standard, and moved to the v1 API version.
The v1alpha2 version of each was deprecated as of the v1.6 release, and will be removed in a future release.
How it works
A Gateway needs a listener that allows TCPRoute attachment:
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: example-gateway
spec:
  gatewayClassName: example-gateway-class
  listeners:
    - name: foo
      protocol: TCP
      port: 12345
      allowedRoutes:
        kinds:
          - kind: TCPRoute
A TCPRoute then attaches to that listener and forwards traffic to a backend:
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: TCPRoute
metadata:
  name: tcp-app
spec:
  parentRefs:
    - name: example-gateway
      sectionName: foo
  rules:
    - backendRefs:
        - name: my-foo-service
          port: 6000
Traffic arriving on the Gateway's port 12345 is proxied to the endpoints of my-foo-service on port 6000. Omitting sectionName and port from parentRefs attaches the route to every TCP listener on the Gateway instead of a single one.
UDPRoute follows the same pattern; swap the listener protocol and the route kind:
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: example-gateway
spec:
  gatewayClassName: example-gateway-class
  listeners:
    - name: foo
      protocol: UDP
      port: 12345
      allowedRoutes:
        kinds:
          - kind: UDPRoute
---
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: UDPRoute
metadata:
  name: udp-app
spec:
  parentRefs:
    - name: example-gateway
      sectionName: foo
  rules:
    - backendRefs:
        - name: my-foo-service
          port: 6000
XBackend arrives in Experimental
Leads: Keith Mattix II
Gateway API v1.6 introduces the new XBackend resource, which is a general-purpose decorator for Service (and other backend types) within Gateway API.
The Service resource is an amazing, stable, and flexible object, but that comes with some costs: The flexibility creates a lot of edge cases that Gateway API needs to handle, and the stability makes it impossible to add new concepts to Service.
The XBackend resource builds on the ideas in the upstream EndpointSelector KEP, to add a Gateway API-native object that still targets the backend app, while allowing the community to extend it to handle use cases that are difficult or dangerous to handle with Service.
The first version of XBackend includes support for ExternalHostname destinations, which are ruled out from Service support in Gateway API because of the possibility of confused deputy attacks.
For XBackend, this support is an Extended/Optional feature, allowing implementations and users to opt in once they understand the security tradeoffs.
This support is very useful for egress use cases (which are most commonly used for cluster-hosted agentic workloads), which the community is also working towards formalizing in GEPs about Gateways for Egress (work in progress, stay tuned!)
The XBackend API is experimental and its behavior can change, do not assume it is ready for production
An example of a Gateway with an ExternalName backend that can be used for egress to a cloud AI API is as follows:
# Gateway-level TLS remains authoritative for incoming connections
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
spec:
  listeners:
  - name: https
    protocol: HTTPS
    tls:
      certificateRefs:
      - name: gateway-cert
---
# Backend resource for external destination
apiVersion: gateway.networking.x-k8s.io/v1alpha1
kind: XBackend
metadata:
  name: ai-provider-api
  namespace: ai-apps
spec:
  type: ExternalHostname
  externalHostname:
    hostname: api.ai-provider.com
---
# HTTPRoute referencing XBackend
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
spec:
  rules:
  - backendRefs:
    - name: ai-provider-api
      kind: XBackend
      group: gateway.networking.x-k8s.io
The community is also working on moving Session Persistence config from XBackendTrafficPolicy into XBackend, along with other use cases like retries, TLS origination and similar config that is useful to be able to configure per-application rather than per-Route.
Experimental resources move off the standard API group
Previously, experimental resources shared the same API group as standard ones - gateway.networking.k8s.io - distinguished only by a v1alpha2-style version. TCPRoute and UDPRoute were the last resources to graduate under that scheme.
Going forward, new experimental resources are defined in a separate group,
gateway.networking.x-k8s.io,
and the names of their API types get an X prefix - for example XBackend and XMesh.
When one of these graduates to Standard, it's renamed into the gateway.networking.k8s.io group
and drops the X prefix, the same way XMesh is expected to become Mesh.
This separation makes the experimental/standard boundary explicit at the API group level, rather than relying on version strings alone.
What's next & getting involved
The graduation of TCPRoute and UDPRoute to Standard marks an essential milestone in making Gateway API a complete, universal ingress and mesh networking API for Kubernetes workloads across layer 4 and layer 7 protocols.
Try it out
You can start using Gateway API v1.6.0 today with your favorite Gateway controller implementation:
- Check out the Gateway API Documentation for detailed guides and API references.
- View the v1.6.0 Release Notes for complete details on the CRD installation and changes.
Gateway API relies on an extensive conformance test suite to ensure consistent, portable behavior across all implementations. Here is a list of the implementations that are conforment with v1.6 on the day we published the article:
Get involved
Gateway API is an open, community-driven project built under Kubernetes SIG Network. We welcome contributions, feedback, and participation from everyone!
- Join our Slack Channel: Join #sig-network-gateway-api on the Kubernetes Slack.
- Attend Community Meetings: We hold weekly community meetings. Check out the SIG Network Calendar for dates and agendas.
- Contribute on GitHub: File issues, suggest enhancements (GEPs), or submit PRs at kubernetes-sigs/gateway-api.
Acknowledgments
A huge thank you to all the contributors, reviewers, maintainers, and implementation authors whose hard work made Gateway API v1.6.0 possible!

title: Go Turns 17
text:
The Go Blog
Go Turns 17
Today, November 10th, we celebrate the 17th anniversary of Go’s open source release!
Over the past year, we released Go 1.26 in February and Go 1.27
in August, alongside a steady stream of releases across our
golang.org/x libraries and developer tools.
Meanwhile, the pace of change across the software industry continues to
accelerate, driven by shifting hardware, evolving security threats, and the
rapid rise of AI-assisted development and agentic systems.
In a tumultuous time for the industry, Go aims to be a steady hand on the tiller. Our goal is to keep Go grounded in its foundational principles of simplicity, reliability, efficiency, and an unwavering commitment to compatibility, while adapting to modern hardware, production workloads, and developer workflows. Increasingly, our investments serve a dual purpose: what helps human engineers write, understand, and maintain reliable Go code at scale also provides the guardrails and authoritative context that AI coding assistants and agents need to be effective.
Core language and library improvements
In the language itself, Go 1.26 and 1.27 addressed several long-standing
restrictions in generics and everyday Go syntax, guided by years of real-world
experience. When generics first landed in Go 1.18, methods could not declare
their own type parameters, which sometimes forced awkward package-level
functions and “inside-out” nested calls. Go 1.27 introduced generic
methods on non-interface types (such as the new
Rand.N method in math/rand/v2),
allowing APIs to stay naturally organized on types and enabling readable method
chaining. Together with support for self-referential type constraints in Go 1.26
and broader type inference for generic function values in Go 1.27, generics in
Go feel more complete and natural than ever.
Alongside generics, two refinements to value construction make everyday Go code
cleaner and more concise. Go 1.26 extended the built-in new function to
accept an initial value expression, allowing new(42)
or new("go1.26") without the ubiquitous newInt-style helper functions used
to populate optional pointer fields in JSON and protocol buffer structs. And in
Go 1.27, struct literal keys can refer directly to fields of embedded or nested
structs, reducing boilerplate in composite literals.
In the standard library, our focus has been on evolving Go’s “production stack”
and eliminating subtle operational traps. Few packages are as central to that as
encoding/json, which has been a mainstay of Go since before Go 1.0. While its
core model has held up remarkably well for over 15 years, tighter JSON standards
and security expectations have turned some of its original defaults into
interoperability and security hazards, such as silently accepting invalid UTF-8
or duplicate object keys and matching struct fields case-insensitively. At
the same time, its buffered design prevented true streaming and limited
performance. Addressing these issues while upholding Go’s compatibility promise
for the millions of existing programs that depend on encoding/json meant
designing a new major version of the package.
Six years in the making, the new encoding/json/v2 and
encoding/json/jsontext packages reached general
availability in Go 1.27. Driven by Joe Tsai, Daniel Martí, and contributors from
across the Go community, this modern JSON API brings safer,
stricter defaults, flexible caller- and type-specified customization, and up to
10× faster unmarshaling, while cleanly separating high-level semantic marshaling
(json/v2) from low-level, reflection-free syntactic streaming (jsontext).
Crucially, we didn’t leave existing code behind: the original
encoding/json package is now implemented entirely in
terms of v2 under the hood. Existing v1 callers get faster unmarshaling
simply by upgrading, and packages using v1 and v2 interoperate seamlessly so
that the ecosystem can migrate gradually without flag days.
We’ve also brought new production diagnostics to Go’s concurrency primitives.
Concurrency is one of Go’s greatest strengths, but goroutines accidentally left
blocked on abandoned channels or locks can silently leak memory and CPU in
long-running services, and traditional goroutine profiles cannot distinguish
leaked goroutines from ones legitimately waiting for work. First previewed in Go
1.26 and now generally available in Go 1.27, the new goroutine leak
profiler (goroutineleak in runtime/pprof and
/debug/pprof/goroutineleak in net/http/pprof) solves this for production
services. Contributed by Vlad Saioc and Uber’s Programming Systems team,
building on academic research with Aarhus University and Washington University
in St. Louis, the profiler repurposes the garbage collector’s reachability phase
to identify goroutines blocked on concurrency primitives that no runnable
goroutine can ever reach. That allows it to pinpoint leaks in production with
near-zero false positives and zero overhead when not in use.
In net/http, closing an HTTP/1 response body with even a single unread
byte—such as a trailing newline left behind by a JSON decoder—previously forced
the client to tear down the underlying TCP and TLS connection. Go 1.27’s HTTP
transport now automatically drains small unread response bodies in the
background on close, turning a widespread latency
footgun into up to a 5× speedup for sequential HTTP/1 requests while letting
application code stay clean and simple.
These releases also added several notable standard library APIs, including a
native uuid package, a generic and type-safe
errors.AsType, and an in-memory
httptest.NewTestServer designed for
virtual-time testing with testing/synctest. Existing
packages saw significant speedups as well: io.ReadAll now
runs twice as fast while allocating half as much memory,
compress/flate compresses faster (speeding up gzip,
zip, zlib, and png), and image/jpeg has a faster,
more accurate encoder and decoder.
Making the most of modern hardware
Modern CPUs look very different from the hardware Go first launched on 17 years ago, with wide vector units and deep, non-uniform memory hierarchies. A major focus of our runtime and compiler work is ensuring Go programs make full use of modern silicon, both transparently when you upgrade your toolchain and through new APIs when you need explicit control.
After debuting as an experiment in Go 1.25, the Green Tea garbage
collector became the default in Go 1.26. By organizing object
marking around contiguous memory spans rather than chasing pointers across the
heap, Green Tea aligns with modern CPU memory architectures to reduce garbage
collection overhead by 10–40% in real-world workloads—and by an additional ~10%
on recent amd64 processors using AVX-512 vector instructions during scanning.
Of course, the runtime shouldn’t be the only part of a Go program that can tap
into vector hardware. Without access to Single Instruction, Multiple Data (SIMD)
capabilities, compute-intensive software, from cryptography and media processing
to data analytics and AI, leaves a significant portion of modern silicon dark.
Until recently, the only way to light up that hardware in Go was by writing and
maintaining per-architecture assembly. To change that, Go 1.26 and 1.27
introduced two experimental SIMD packages: simd/archsimd,
for low-level access to architecture-specific vector instructions on amd64,
arm64 (NEON), and WebAssembly (wasm); and simd, a
higher-level, width-agnostic API that provides portable, near-assembly
performance across architectures with automatic fallback emulation.
We’ve also attacked the cost of memory allocation from multiple angles. The
cheapest heap allocation is the one that never happens: in Go 1.26, the compiler
began allocating initial slice backing stores on the
stack at append sites—even for slices that
ultimately escape to the heap—eliminating the flurry of small heap allocations
that typically accompany slice growth. And for heap allocations more broadly, Go
1.27 introduced size-specialized memory
allocation to speed up allocating the small
objects (such as small structs, slices, and strings) that dominate allocator
time. Generating dedicated fast-path allocator routines for size classes up to
80 bytes made small allocations up to 30% faster and improved overall
performance in allocation-heavy programs. Together with a ~30% reduction in
baseline cgo call overhead in Go 1.26, these improvements make Go programs
faster and leaner out of the box.
Secure software and ecosystem defense
Go’s approach to security spans the entire lifecycle of software: providing safe APIs by design, preparing cryptography for the future, and actively defending the live ecosystem as new threats emerge.
To defend against store-now, decrypt-later attacks and support the industry’s
accelerating timelines for quantum readiness, Go has continued expanding its
post-quantum cryptography support. Go 1.26 enabled hybrid post-quantum key
exchanges (SecP256r1MLKEM768 and SecP384r1MLKEM1024) by default in
crypto/tls and added the crypto/hpke package
(implementing RFC 9180 Hybrid Public Key Encryption, including post-quantum
hybrid KEMs). Go 1.27 followed up with the new
crypto/mldsa package, implementing the FIPS 204
post-quantum ML-DSA signature standard and integrating it into crypto/x509 and
crypto/tls.
At the same time, we’ve continued hardening the standard library and runtime
against subtle classes of vulnerabilities. Most key generation and signing
functions across Go’s crypto/... packages now unconditionally draw from a
secure system randomness source, closing off a classic footgun where
non-cryptographic readers were accidentally passed in. Under the hood, Go 1.26
also added 64-bit heap base address randomization to harden cgo binaries and
introduced the experimental runtime/secret package for
eagerly erasing sensitive cryptographic temporaries from registers, stack
frames, and the heap.
Securing Go deployments also requires rapid vulnerability and incident response
in a fast-moving threat landscape. From the Go vulnerability database and
govulncheck to our
release infrastructure, we’ve invested heavily in ecosystem defense. In October,
that preparation was put to the test during the eMudhra certificate key
disclosure incident, when eight intermediate TLS and
code-signing certificates chaining to a widely trusted root CA were discovered
to use trivially weak private keys. Because Linux lacks a uniform OS-level
certificate revocation mechanism, Go’s built-in TLS verifier is the frontline
defense for millions of Linux services. Within seven and a half hours of initial
notification, the Go Security team shipped a targeted block in our first-ever
URGENT track security release (Go 1.27.3 and Go
1.26.10) alongside an updated Go vulnerability database entry so govulncheck
could flag affected binaries, giving Go users everything they needed to protect
their deployments before the weak keys were publicly disclosed the next morning.
Advancing the broader Go platform and tooling
Go has always been more than a compiler and standard library: it is an
end-to-end platform for software engineering. Over the past year, our work in
golang.org/x/tools, the
gopls language server, vscode-go,
and pkg.go.dev has focused on making that platform even
more productive for both human developers and AI coding assistants.
In last fall’s Go Developer Survey, the single biggest challenge developers reported was ensuring their code follows best practices and current Go idioms. As Go evolves while standing by its compatibility promise, older ways of writing code continue to work alongside newer, clearer, or faster alternatives, creating a natural drift in idioms over time. That drift has been compounded by AI coding assistants, which gravitate toward the older patterns that dominate their training data.
Go 1.26 tackled this with a complete overhaul of the go fix
command, returning the long-dormant tool to its pre-Go 1.0
roots to apply dozens of automatic
modernizers
across entire codebases. What gofmt did for stylistic consistency, modernizers
aim to do for idiomatic consistency. Available both as instant suggestions in
gopls and as bulk, push-button upgrades in go fix, modernizers simplify
existing code and help developers discover new language and library features. We
now routinely consider whether new language and library proposals should ship
with a modernizer of their own. Just as importantly, modernizers give coding
agents an immediate way to bring generated code up to date, while helping shift
the global corpus of open source Go code so that future models learn modern
idioms from the start.
Bespoke modernizers work well for the language and standard library, but a
centralized team can never write them for every third-party module in the
ecosystem. That’s why Go 1.26 also introduced the annotation-driven
source-level inliner, the first step toward a “self-service”
paradigm for automated code maintenance. Any package author can now annotate a
deprecated function, type, or constant with //go:fix inline, and the inliner
will safely migrate callers and references via go fix or in the IDE, carefully
handling evaluation order, side effects, and name shadowing.
In the editor, we’ve made four feature-packed releases of gopls over the past
year (v0.21.0, v0.22.0,
v0.23.0, and v0.24.0). In
collaboration with the Dart team, we designed and proposed an open Language
Server Protocol (LSP) extension for interactive
refactoring, allowing language servers to ask
for user input through dynamic, multi-step dialogs in any supporting editor. Now
integrated into gopls and vscode-go, interactive refactoring powers
customizable struct tag addition and removal, interface implementation
(including generic interfaces) with live symbol search, and cross-package
declaration moves. Beyond refactoring, gopls also gained generalized package
renaming across directories, zero-configuration support for editing Go assembly
files, subexpression hover inspection, completions and inlay hints for promoted
fields, automatic govulncheck scanning when go.mod dependencies change, and
continued enhancements to its built-in Model Context Protocol (MCP)
server for AI coding assistants.
Rounding out the developer platform, in May we launched the official
pkg.go.dev API and followed up with support for
go doc pkg@version in Go 1.27. Previously, developer
tools and IDE integrations had to resort to fragile web scraping to query
ecosystem metadata. Today, the pkg.go.dev API gives tool authors and AI coding
agents a fast, authoritative service for querying module versions, package
symbols, importers, and vulnerability data, while go doc pkg@version makes it
easy to pull up documentation for any version of any package right from the
command line.
Looking ahead
We have an ambitious year ahead for Go.
On the tooling front, we’re building on the pkg.go.dev API, gopls, and go fix to make Go’s developer tools even more capable for both human developers
and coding agents. Following the strong community response to go fix and
//go:fix inline, we’re exploring ways to expand self-service static
analysis, enabling developers, package maintainers, and
organizations to easily integrate custom analyzers and domain-specific
best-practice checks directly into their development workflows. We’re also
exploring ways to surface richer package health and quality signals on
pkg.go.dev and through its API, helping developers and coding agents evaluate
and choose trustworthy, reliable dependencies.
In the language and libraries, Go 1.28 will resolve one of Go’s longest-standing
language requests by allowing composite literals to omit redundant
types whenever the type can be inferred from context, cutting
visual noise in deeply nested configurations, API requests, and table-driven
tests. And with recent generics refinements and hashing
APIs in place, we’ve just accepted a
swath of proposals for generic collection APIs—including sets,
ordered maps, and more—which will land in golang.org/x/exp over the next few
weeks so the community can try them out and share feedback ahead of future
standard library inclusion.
Under the hood, we’re working hard to graduate a large subset of the simd and
simd/archsimd packages (covering amd64, arm64 NEON, and wasm) in Go
1.28, with further expansions and arm64 scalable vector (SVE) support targeted
for Go 1.29. Amid the global RAM crunch, reducing Go’s memory footprint is also
one of our major priorities for the coming year.
In the toolchain, Go 1.28 will increase build parallelism by writing compiler
export data early and streamline static analysis by decoupling
tool export data from the compiler. Looking further out, we’re
working to support cgo builds without requiring a C toolchain,
and we’re kicking the tires on WebAssembly’s early-stage stack-switching
extension, which is already showing promising improvements in Go Wasm
performance and binary size.
Finally, ensuring Go stands the test of time means scaling not just our
technology, but the open source project itself. Over the past year, some of Go’s
most impactful advances, including encoding/json/v2 and the goroutineleak
profile, were driven by or built in close partnership with contributors outside
Google. To better support our growing ecosystem and contributor base, we’re
working to bridge the gap between Go maintainers at Google and our broader
community, and to diversify Go’s technical stewardship. That includes
restructuring the proposal process to improve throughput, give
the community clearer visibility into the process and input into prioritization,
and formally involve community contributors in triage and review. Beyond
proposals, we are building a clearer contributor ladder to empower proven
contributors with greater autonomy, decision-making privileges, and maintenance
responsibilities, and opening up maintainer summits and day-to-day
communications to trusted contributors from our amazing community.
Seventeen years in, Go is thriving because of the people who use it, build with it, and contribute to it every day. Thank you to everyone in the Go community for being part of this journey, and we wish you all the best in the year ahead!

title: A new Go API for JSON
text:
The Go Blog
A new Go API for JSON
Introduction
JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) is a simple data interchange format, the most popular data format used on the internet, and widely read and written by Go programs. Go has included support for JSON in the standard library since well before Go 1.0. We first wrote about support for JSON in Go more than 15 years ago!
Over time, packages evolve with the needs of their users, and encoding/json is no exception.
Last year, we wrote about a new experimental API for JSON designed to bring long-awaited improvements and fixes.
After additional feedback and refinement, the new encoding/json/v2 and encoding/json/jsontext packages are stable and generally available in Go 1.27!
This post is an updated version of the article introducing the experiment, describing the problems with encoding/json and introducing the new packages.
Problems with encoding/json
Overall, encoding/json has held up well.
The idea of marshaling and unmarshaling arbitrary Go types
with some default representation in JSON, combined with the ability to
customize the representation, has proven to be highly flexible.
However, in the years since its introduction,
various users have identified numerous shortcomings.
Behavior flaws
There are various behavioral flaws in encoding/json:
- Imprecise handling of JSON syntax: Over the years, JSON has seen increased standardization in order for programs to properly communicate. Generally, decoders have become stricter at rejecting ambiguous inputs, to reduce the chance that two implementations will have different (successful) interpretations of a particular JSON value. 
  - encoding/json currently accepts invalid UTF-8,
whereas the latest Internet Standard (RFC 8259) requires valid UTF-8.
The default behavior should report an error in the presence of invalid UTF-8,
instead of introducing silent data corruption,
which may cause problems downstream.
  - encoding/json currently accepts objects with duplicate member names.
RFC 8259 does not specify how to handle duplicate names,
so an implementation is free to choose an arbitrary value,
merge the values, discard the values, or report an error.
The presence of a duplicate name results in a JSON value
without a universally agreed upon meaning.
This could be exploited by attackers in security applications
and has been exploited before (as in CVE-2017-12635).
The default behavior should err on the side of safety and reject duplicate names.
- Leaking nilness of slices and maps: JSON is often used to communicate with
programs using JSON implementations that do not allow null to be unmarshaled
into a data type expected to be a JSON array or object.
Since encoding/json marshals a nil slice or map as a JSON null,
this may lead to errors when unmarshaling by other implementations.
A survey
indicated that most Go users prefer that nil slices and maps
are marshaled as an empty JSON array or object by default.
- Case-insensitive unmarshaling: When unmarshaling, a JSON object member name is resolved to a Go struct field name using a case-insensitive match. This is a surprising default, a potential security vulnerability, and a performance limitation.
- Inconsistent calling of methods: Due to an implementation detail,
MarshalJSON methods declared on a pointer receiver
are inconsistently called by encoding/json. While regarded as a bug,
this cannot be fixed as too many applications depend on the current behavior.
API deficiencies
The API of encoding/json can be tricky or restrictive:
- It is difficult to correctly unmarshal from an io.Reader.
Users often write json.NewDecoder(r).Decode(v),
which fails to reject trailing junk at the end of the input.
- Options can be set on the Encoder and Decoder types,
but cannot be used with the Marshal and Unmarshal functions.
Similarly, types implementing the Marshaler and Unmarshaler interfaces
cannot make use of the options and there is no way to plumb options down the call stack.
For example, the Decoder.DisallowUnknownFields option loses its effect
when calling a custom UnmarshalJSON method.
- The Compact, Indent, and HTMLEscape functions write to a bytes.Buffer instead of something more flexible like a []byte or io.Writer.
This limits the usability of those functions.
Performance limitations
Setting aside internal implementation details, the public API commits it to certain performance limitations:
- MarshalJSON: The MarshalJSON interface method forces the implementation
to allocate the returned []byte. Also, the semantics require that encoding/json verify that the result is valid JSON
and also to reformat it to match the specified indentation.
- UnmarshalJSON: The UnmarshalJSON interface method requires that
a complete JSON value be provided (without any trailing data).
This forces encoding/json to parse the JSON value to be unmarshaled
in its entirety to determine where it ends before it can call UnmarshalJSON.
Afterwards, the UnmarshalJSON method itself must parse the provided JSON value again.
- Lack of streaming: Even though the Encoder and Decoder types operate
on an io.Writer or io.Reader, they buffer the entire JSON value in memory.
The Decoder.Token method for reading individual tokens is allocation-heavy
and there is no corresponding API for writing tokens.
Furthermore, if the implementation of a MarshalJSON or UnmarshalJSON method
recursively calls the Marshal or Unmarshal function,
then the performance becomes quadratic.
Trying to fix encoding/json directly
Introducing a new, incompatible major version of a package is a heavy consideration. If possible, we should try to fix the existing package.
While it is relatively easy to add new features, it is difficult to change existing features. Unfortunately, these problems are inherent consequences of the existing API, making them practically impossible to fix within the Go 1 compatibility promise.
We could in principle declare separate names, such as MarshalV2 or UnmarshalV2,
but that is tantamount to creating a parallel namespace within the same package.
This leads us to encoding/json/v2 (henceforth called v2),
where we can make these changes within a separate v2 namespace
in contrast to encoding/json (henceforth called v1).
Building on encoding/json/jsontext
Before discussing the v2 API, we first introduce the
encoding/json/jsontext package
that lays the foundation for improvements to JSON in Go.
JSON serialization in Go can be broken down into two primary components:
- syntactic functionality that is concerned with processing JSON based on its grammar, and
- semantic functionality that defines the relationship between JSON values and Go values.
We use the terms “encode” and “decode” to describe syntactic functionality and the terms “marshal” and “unmarshal” to describe semantic functionality. We aim to provide a clear distinction between functionality that is purely concerned with encoding versus that of marshaling.
This diagram provides an overview of this separation.
Purple blocks represent types, while blue blocks represent functions or methods.
The direction of the arrows approximately represents the flow of data.
The bottom half of the diagram, implemented by the jsontext package,
contains functionality that is only concerned with syntax,
while the upper half, implemented by the json/v2 package,
contains functionality that assigns semantic meaning to syntactic data
handled by the bottom half.
The basic API of jsontext is the following:
package jsontext
type Encoder struct { ... }
func NewEncoder(io.Writer, ...Options) *Encoder
func (*Encoder) WriteValue(Value) error
func (*Encoder) WriteToken(Token) error
type Decoder struct { ... }
func NewDecoder(io.Reader, ...Options) *Decoder
func (*Decoder) ReadValue() (Value, error)
func (*Decoder) ReadToken() (Token, error)
type Kind byte
type Value []byte
func (Value) Kind() Kind
type Token struct { ... }
func (Token) Kind() Kind
The jsontext package provides functionality for interacting with JSON
at a syntactic level and derives its name from
RFC 8259, section 2
where the grammar for JSON data is literally called JSON-text.
Since it only interacts with JSON at a syntactic level,
it does not depend on Go reflection.
The Encoder and
Decoder
provide support for encoding and decoding JSON values and tokens.
The constructors
accept variadic options
that affect the particular behavior of encoding and decoding.
Unlike the Encoder and Decoder types declared in v1,
the new types in jsontext avoid muddling the distinction between syntax and
semantics and operate in a truly streaming manner.
A JSON value is a complete unit of data and is represented in Go as
a named []byte.
It is identical to RawMessage in v1, which is now a type alias to jsontext.Value.
A JSON value is syntactically composed of one or more JSON tokens.
A JSON token is represented in Go as the opaque Token type
with constructors and accessor methods.
It is analogous to Token in v1
but is designed to represent arbitrary JSON tokens without allocation.
To resolve the fundamental performance problems with
the MarshalJSON and UnmarshalJSON interface methods,
we need an efficient way of encoding and decoding JSON
as a streaming sequence of tokens and values.
In v2, we introduce the MarshalJSONTo and UnmarshalJSONFrom interface methods
that operate on an Encoder or Decoder, allowing the methods’ implementations
to process JSON in a purely streaming manner. Thus, the json package need not
be responsible for validating or formatting a JSON value returned by MarshalJSON,
nor would it need to be responsible for determining the boundaries of a JSON value
provided to UnmarshalJSON. These responsibilities belong to the Encoder and Decoder.
Introducing encoding/json/v2
Building on the jsontext package, we now introduce the
encoding/json/v2 package.
It is designed to fix the problems in v1,
while remaining familiar to users of the v1 package.
Our goal is that usages of v1 will operate mostly the same if directly migrated to v2.
Here, we primarily cover the high-level API of v2.
For examples on how to use it, we encourage readers to
study the examples in the v2 package,
the “Working with JSON” tutorial, or
read Anton Zhiyanov’s blog covering the topic.
The basic API of v2 is the following:
package json
func Marshal(in any, opts ...Options) (out []byte, err error)
func MarshalWrite(out io.Writer, in any, opts ...Options) error
func MarshalEncode(out *jsontext.Encoder, in any, opts ...Options) error
func Unmarshal(in []byte, out any, opts ...Options) error
func UnmarshalRead(in io.Reader, out any, opts ...Options) error
func UnmarshalDecode(in *jsontext.Decoder, out any, opts ...Options) error
The Marshal
and Unmarshal functions
have a signature similar to v1, but accept options to configure their behavior.
The MarshalWrite
and UnmarshalRead functions
directly operate on an io.Writer or io.Reader,
avoiding the need to temporarily construct an Encoder or Decoder
just to write or read from such types.
The MarshalEncode
and UnmarshalDecode functions
operate on a jsontext.Encoder and jsontext.Decoder and
are actually the underlying implementation of the previously mentioned functions.
Unlike v1, options are a first-class argument to each of the marshal and unmarshal functions,
greatly extending the flexibility and configurability of v2.
There are several options available
in v2 which are not covered by this article.
Type-specified customization
Similar to v1, v2 allows types to define their own JSON representation
by satisfying particular interfaces.
type Marshaler interface {
    MarshalJSON() ([]byte, error)
}
type MarshalerTo interface {
    MarshalJSONTo(*jsontext.Encoder) error
}
type Unmarshaler interface {
    UnmarshalJSON([]byte) error
}
type UnmarshalerFrom interface {
    UnmarshalJSONFrom(*jsontext.Decoder) error
}
The Marshaler
and Unmarshaler interfaces
are identical to those in v1.
The new MarshalerTo
and UnmarshalerFrom interfaces
allow a type to represent itself as JSON using a jsontext.Encoder or jsontext.Decoder.
This allows options to be forwarded down the call stack, since options
can be retrieved via the Options accessor method on the Encoder or Decoder.
See the OrderedObject example
for how to implement a custom type that maintains the ordering of JSON object members.
Caller-specified customization
In v2, the caller of Marshal and Unmarshal can also specify
a custom JSON representation for any arbitrary type,
where caller-specified functions take precedence over type-defined methods
or the default representation for a particular type.
func WithMarshalers(*Marshalers) Options
type Marshalers struct { ... }
func MarshalFunc[T any](fn func(T) ([]byte, error)) *Marshalers
func MarshalToFunc[T any](fn func(*jsontext.Encoder, T) error) *Marshalers
func WithUnmarshalers(*Unmarshalers) Options
type Unmarshalers struct { ... }
func UnmarshalFunc[T any](fn func([]byte, T) error) *Unmarshalers
func UnmarshalFromFunc[T any](fn func(*jsontext.Decoder, T) error) *Unmarshalers
MarshalFunc and
MarshalToFunc
construct a custom marshaler that can be passed to a Marshal call
using WithMarshalers to override the marshaling of particular types.
Similarly,
UnmarshalFunc and
UnmarshalFromFunc
support similar customization for Unmarshal.
The ProtoJSON example
demonstrates how this feature allows serialization of all
proto.Message types
to be handled by the protojson package.
Behavior differences
While v2 aims to behave mostly the same as v1,
its behavior has changed in some ways
to address problems in v1, most notably:
- v2 reports an error in the presence of invalid UTF-8.
- v2 reports an error if a JSON object contains a duplicate name.
- v2 marshals a nil Go slice or Go map as an empty JSON array or JSON object, respectively.
- v2 unmarshals a JSON object into a Go struct using a
case-sensitive match from the JSON member name to the Go field name.
- v2 redefines the omitempty tag option to omit a field if it would have
encoded as an “empty” JSON value (which are null, "", [], and {}).
- v2 reports an error when trying to serialize a time.Duration,
which currently has no default representation,
but provides options to let the caller decide.
For most behavior changes, there is a struct tag option or caller-specified option
that can configure the behavior to operate under v1 or v2 semantics,
or even other caller-determined behavior.
See “Migrating to v2” for more information.
Performance optimizations
The Marshal performance of v2 is roughly at parity with v1.
Sometimes it is slightly faster, but other times it is slightly slower.
The Unmarshal performance of v2 is significantly faster than v1,
with benchmarks demonstrating improvements of up to 10x.
In order to obtain greater performance gains,
existing implementations of
Marshaler and
Unmarshaler should
migrate to also implement
MarshalerTo and
UnmarshalerFrom,
so that they can benefit from processing JSON in a purely streaming manner.
For example, recursive parsing of OpenAPI specifications in UnmarshalJSON methods
significantly hurt performance in a particular service of Kubernetes
(see kubernetes/kube-openapi#315),
while switching to UnmarshalJSONFrom improved performance by orders of magnitude.
For more benchmark details, see the
go-json-experiment/jsonbench
repository.
On top of structural improvements, we’re continuing to invest in performance optimizations in the implementation for cases where the v2 implementation is slower than v1.
You can expect additional improvements in Go 1.28.
Compatibility
The Go 1 compatibility promise is a core guarantee from the Go project that allows developers to build applications that will stand the test of time and continue working on future versions of Go.
The original encoding/json and new encoding/json/v2 packages are of course both subject to the Go 1 compatibility promise.
Applications using v1 will continue to be supported indefinitely and need not ever migrate to v2.
That said, when designing the v2 packages we wanted to do better than keeping v1 supported.
We wanted to ensure that v1 and v2 are compatible with one another so that packages using different versions can work together.
Doing so allows a smooth ecosystem migration rather than forcing users to use one version or another due to the choices of their dependencies.
For instance, suppose your package uses v2 to marshal a struct containing a field with a type defined in another package.
That package may use the original v1 MarshalJSON method to define its marshaling behavior.
No problem, v2 supports MarshalJSON methods, so marshaling will continue working as expected.
Vice versa, suppose your package uses v1 to marshal the same struct.
The other package may use the v2 MarshalJSONTo method for better performance.
No problem here either, as the v1 implementation supports v2’s MarshalJSONTo method under the hood.
We’ve achieved this by designing the new packages such that, under the hood, v1 is implemented in terms of v2.
As mentioned above, v2 supports a variety of Options.
Each behavior difference is controlled by one of these options.
Thus, v1 can be implemented in terms of v2 by passing the full set of v1 compatibility options.
With this approach, backwards-compatible additions such as new methods (e.g., MarshalJSONTo) or new struct tags (e.g., embed) are automatically supported to the benefit of existing v1 users.
Migration
Implementing v1 in terms of v2 options has the additional benefit of allowing gradual migration of callsites.
encoding/json documents the full set of behavior differences between v1 and v2, and which option controls those behaviors.
Many applications can migrate directly to v2 with no visible behavior changes, but applications that depend on v1 behavior can use the options to change only the behaviors they depend on.
For example, we can select all v2 behavior except that duplicate names are allowed:
json.Marshal(..., json.DefaultOptionsV2(), jsontext.AllowDuplicateNames(true))
Alternatively, we can select all v1 behavior except that duplicate names are disallowed:
json.Marshal(..., jsonv1.DefaultOptionsV1(), jsontext.AllowDuplicateNames(false))
The encoding/json/v2 Migration Guide goes into more detail, covering a variety of scenarios for approaching migration of an application from v1 to v2.
More information
For additional references on working with the new JSON packages, see:
- The “Working with JSON” tutorial,
- The encoding/json/v2 and encoding/json/jsontext package documentation,
- The encoding/json package’s v2 comparison documentation,
- and the encoding/json/v2 Migration Guide.
A long time coming
The planning for a new major version of encoding/json spanned years.
In late 2020, spurred on by the inability to fix issues in the current package,
Daniel Martí (one of the maintainers of encoding/json) first drafted his
thoughts on what a hypothetical v2 package should look like.
Separately, after previous work on the Go API for Protocol Buffers,
Joe Tsai was disappointed that the protojson package
needed to use a custom JSON implementation because encoding/json was
neither capable of adhering to the stricter JSON standard that the
Protocol Buffer specification required,
nor of efficiently serializing JSON in a streaming manner.
Believing a brighter future for JSON was both beneficial and achievable,
Daniel and Joe joined forces to brainstorm on v2 and
started to build a prototype
(with the initial code being a polished version of the JSON serialization logic from the Go protobuf module).
Over time, a few others (Roger Peppe, Chris Hines, Johan Brandhorst-Satzkorn, Damien Neil, Austin Clements, and Michael Pratt)
joined the effort by providing design review, code review, and regression testing.
Many of the early discussions are publicly available in our
recorded meetings and
meeting notes.
Later discussions are available in our encoding/json/v2 working group meeting notes.
This work has been public since the beginning,
and we increasingly involved the wider Go community,
first with a
GopherCon talk and
discussion posted in late 2023,
formal proposal posted in early 2025,
and finally adopting encoding/json/v2 as a Go experiment in Go 1.25
for wider-scale testing by all Go users.
The v2 effort took about 6 years to reach this point,
incorporating feedback from many contributors and also gaining valuable
empirical experience from use in production settings.
It’s worth noting that it’s largely been developed and promoted by people not employed by Google, demonstrating that the Go project is a collaborative endeavor with a thriving global community dedicated to improving the Go ecosystem.
Thank you to everyone that contributed!

title: Our Response To The eMudhra Key Disclosure Incident
text:
The Go Blog
Our Response To The eMudhra Key Disclosure Incident
On October 19, the Go team initiated an expedited security release to protect Go users and their applications from a critical public key infrastructure (PKI) compromise involving certificates issued by eMudhra.
Within approximately seven and a half hours of being notified, we shipped a targeted patch, which was included in our first-ever URGENT track security release.
Here is the context behind the incident, why Go stepped in at the runtime level to protect our users and how our incident response unfolded.
eMudhra Incident
On October 17, Mozilla added eight intermediate certificates (six used for TLS, and two used for code signing) issued by a root certificate controlled by eMudhra to OneCRL, effectively blocking their usage in Firefox. Soon after, a number of security researchers noticed this and began investigating what might’ve caused this.
On October 19, the Go Security team was made aware of these investigations and their conclusions, which showed that the keys associated with these intermediates were trivially weak, allowing recovery of the private keys in microseconds.
Due to the fact that the eMudhra root certificate was present in most trusted root programs, recovering the private keys would allow any attacker to sign arbitrary TLS certificates for any domain name, without the usual requirement to show proof of control of said domain name. This would allow an attacker to man-in-the-middle (MITM) TLS connections and present a valid certificate for a domain name they did not control, effectively allowing them to impersonate any TLS server the targeted machine attempted to connect to.
Go ships a TLS certificate verifier in the standard library. When users use net/http or crypto/tls to connect to a TLS service, the verifier is called to check if the certificates the other side of the connection presents are valid. On Windows and macOS we delegate these checks to the platform APIs, and on Linux, which lacks platform APIs, we use our own verifier implementation.
Since Linux does not have a uniform built-in mechanism to handle revocation checking, and in order to provide a timely fix for users on other platforms that might not receive platform updates, we decided the best way to protect Go users was to do an URGENT track security release which similarly removed trust.
Incident Timeline
A typical Go security release follows a multi-day process, with advanced pre-announcements in order to allow those who rely on Go to prepare. In this case, because we believed that private key exposure was imminent, our team chose to use the URGENT track for the first time in order to ship protections before active public exploitation could begin.
11:45 PDT
Our Security team was alerted by an independent external researcher, citing unreported actions by Mozilla and other organizations to remove trust in eight eMudhra intermediates. It became clear quickly that this was due to weak private keys they used.
12:30 PDT
Mozilla independently reported the issue to our Security team, confirming the issue, and asking that we not immediately disclose the issue, but encouraging us to release a fix as soon as possible.
14:00 PDT
We finalized a patch which blocked the usage of certificates which chained to the compromised intermediates, and thanks to the researcher who initially alerted us to the issue, had a set of certificates signed using the recovered keys to test against.
15:00 PDT
We began the process to release minor Go versions 1.27.3 and 1.26.10 containing our patch. Due to the urgent nature of this issue and its exploitability, and with the belief that the private keys would likely become publicly known within hours, we decided an immediate release was the most prudent option.
19:13 PDT
We finalized the release and announced it publicly. At this time the underlying issue was still not widely known. In an effort to give other defenders a chance to protect as many users as possible without revealing to attackers how the issue could be exploited, our patch and communications were somewhat opaque, warning users that we were “blocking trust in a small set of intermediate certificates due to specific security concerns around their operation” and urging users to immediately upgrade to this release.
In under seven and a half hours from initial notification, patched Go releases were live worldwide, giving users everything they needed to secure their deployments before the keys became public.
By the morning of October 20, numerous independent researchers had publicly disclosed the weak keys.
Lessons Learned and Future Improvements
This was our first ever URGENT track security release, and during the release process we ran into a number of issues which caused the release to take longer than expected.
While we are happy we were able to get a release out the same day we were notified of the issue, in the modern security environment we feel that we should be able to provide releases in a more compressed timeline. The issues we ran into caused our release process to take just under four and a quarter hours from start to finish.
These issues had previously not been problematic, since the typical release process is split up over a number of days.
We’ve subsequently made a number of changes to improve our release efficiency, which should significantly reduce the time it takes us to push out a release, enhancing our ability to quickly respond to urgent security threats.
PRIVATE track security fixes are pre-announced three to seven days before their release. URGENT track fixes happen on a shorter time schedule, but we could have pre-announced the upcoming release when we began the release process, giving users at least a few hours to prepare.
While on Windows and macOS we rely on the revocation mechanisms the platform APIs provide, on Linux we don’t currently have a similar mechanism. The lack of this support was one of our major drivers to issue an expedited security release, as we did not want to leave Linux users exposed to this issue longer than was necessary.
Hence we are planning on prioritizing work to bring parity to revocation support on Linux, to help mitigate this class of issues in the future. Part of this work will involve investigating adding support for the upki project, which aims to “provide reliable, privacy-preserving and efficient certificate revocation” for Linux (see issue #82402).
Upgrading and Verifying Your Deployments
If you run Go binaries which interact with network services using TLS (such as directly via net/http or crypto/tls or via a dependency such as gRPC), ensure you are running on the latest minor releases. Binaries rebuilt with Go 1.27.3 and 1.26.10 will automatically reject certificates issued by the compromised eMudhra intermediates.
You can verify your current toolchain version using go version and you can check the version of Go a binary was built with using go version -m <path_to_your_binary>.
The govulncheck tool can also be used to determine if a binary is affected by this issue:
$ GOTOOLCHAIN=go1.27.3+auto go install golang.org/x/vuln/cmd/govulncheck@latest
$ govulncheck -mode=binary <path_to_your_binary>
Securing Go Deployments Everywhere
For us, securing Go and its users extends beyond fixing direct security vulnerabilities in the runtime and libraries we ship. In order to keep the ecosystem secure, we believe we also need to provide users with the right tools to write secure software, look towards the future of cryptographic algorithms and protocols, and proactively respond to ecosystem wide issues when we can.
We are grateful to the independent security researchers and the Mozilla security team for this rapid notification and coordination during this incident.

title: Help set Go's priorities for next year
text:
The Go Blog
Help set Go's priorities for next year
Hi Gophers! The 2026 Go Developer Survey is now open. We run this survey every year to understand how you use Go and the challenges you face. Your answers directly shape how we plan and prioritize our work.
Last year, 5,379 of you responded, and your top frustration was making sure your code follows best practices and Go idioms (33% of respondents). Since then, we shipped a rewritten go fix in Go 1.26 that automatically modernizes your code, and added more modernizers in Go 1.27. You can read everything we learned in the 2025 results.
Take the survey here. It’s open through November 3, takes about 10–20 minutes, and every question is optional. We’ll share the results on this blog in early 2027.
Please share the survey with your colleagues, friends, and online communities—the more Go developers we hear from, the better we understand what you need.
Thank you for helping shape the future of Go!

title: Interactive refactoring in gopls
text:
The Go Blog
Interactive refactoring in gopls
When editing code in a modern IDE or editor, developers rely on its refactoring features to automate common transformations. Today, we are excited to introduce interactive refactoring in gopls, powered by a new capability we are proposing for the Language Server Protocol (LSP) that brings dynamic, multi-step dialogs directly into your favorite editor. Crucially, we designed this capability (in collaboration with the Dart team) not just for Go, but as an open standard for all programming languages and editor ecosystems. Working support is already available in gopls v0.24.0 and the official Go extension for VS Code v0.56.0.
What is the Language Server Protocol (LSP)?
The LSP is an open standard that decouples language-specific features from specific text editors. As you navigate and edit code, your editor (such as VS Code, Neovim, or Emacs) and a language server (like gopls) engage in a continuous JSON-RPC exchange to provide features like autocomplete, hover documentation, diagnostics, and code actions.
Multi-step code transformation
Today, almost every code transformation in the LSP is like a function of no
parameters: you trigger the operation, and the server immediately computes the
edits. (Renaming a symbol is the sole exception: because it is a function of one
parameter, the desired new name, it required its own dedicated PrepareRename
RPC in the protocol.)
"Add struct tags", without questions
The language server must deduce the user’s intent from context alone, namely the cursor position and the enclosing syntax tree. When that context is not enough, the server is forced into one of two choices: apply a one-size-fits-all default, or refrain from offering the transformation altogether. The limitation lies not in gopls’s ability to compute the necessary edits, but in the LSP’s lack of a mechanism for language servers to ask the user for input.
For many transformations, this parameterless model works well. But many others
need additional input from the user: which struct tags to add and in what
naming convention, which interface to implement, which file to move a
declaration to. Without a way to ask, gopls could only guess—“Add struct
tags”, for example, always produced json tags in camelCase—or not offer the
refactoring at all. With interactive refactoring, language servers can now
easily provide new operations with one or more parameters.
"Add struct tags", with questions
While some language extensions have worked around this limitation by embedding custom, language-specific dialog logic directly into individual editors, doing so leaves behind other editors (such as Neovim and Emacs) that stick strictly to the LSP with minimal custom client code. More importantly, editor-specific workarounds go against the fundamental purpose of the LSP: to decouple language-specific features from editors so that each server improvement benefits every client.
Our LSP interactive refactoring proposal (microsoft/language-server-protocol#1164) solves this by establishing a standard mechanism for language servers to collect user input before computing text edits. For Go developers, this unlocks a suite of long-awaited refactorings, including:
- golang/go#70583: Move Declaration
- golang/go#38028: Change Signature
- golang/vscode-go#1547: Implement Interface
- golang/vscode-go#2002: Modify Struct Tags
among many others.
Interactive refactorings in action
Adding and removing struct tags (gopls v0.23.0)
When configuring serialization formats, developers frequently need custom tags
and casing conventions. Previously, running “Add struct tags” unconditionally
injected json tags using camelCase formatting.
With interactive refactoring:
- Place your cursor on any struct definition and select the “Add struct tags” code action.
- An input dialog appears, pre-filled with json, allowing you to customize
any combination of tags (such as json,yaml,db).
- A second dialog lets you select your desired naming convention (such as
camelCase, snake_case, or PascalCase).
- Gopls generates and applies the formatted struct tags across your type definition.
Interactive "Add struct tags" in VS Code
Here is the before-and-after transformation:
type UserProfile struct {
    ID        int64
    FirstName string
    LastName  string
    EmailAddr string
}
type UserProfile struct {
    ID        int64  `json:"id" db:"id"`
    FirstName string `json:"first_name" db:"first_name"`
    LastName  string `json:"last_name" db:"last_name"`
    EmailAddr string `json:"email_addr" db:"email_addr"`
}
Similarly, “Remove struct tags” now asks you for the specific tag keys
you wish to delete (for example, removing only db tags while preserving the json
tag), rather than wiping out all struct tags indiscriminately.
Interactive "Remove struct tags" in VS Code
Implementing interfaces with dynamic symbol search
When creating a type to satisfy an interface, developers previously had to copy
the interface declaration and manually turn it into a set of methods on the
receiver type (or rely on external tools like impl by manually typing the
receiver and qualifying the name of the interface).
Since gopls v0.23.0, with interactive refactoring:
- Place your cursor on any concrete type and select the “Add methods to X to implement an interface…” code action.
- A text entry field appears, inviting you to choose the name of an interface
type. It makes dynamic queries to gopls to auto-complete names of types in
your workspace and the standard library (for example, maphash.Hasher).
- If the selected interface has type parameters, gopls asks for a
concrete type argument for each type parameter (such as Foo).
- Gopls generates complete method stubs with appropriate receiver names and instantiated method signatures.
Interactive "Add methods to implement an interface..." in VS Code
type Foo struct{}
type MyHasher struct{}
type Foo struct{}
type MyHasher struct{}
// Equal implements [maphash.Hasher].
func (m *MyHasher) Equal(x Foo, y Foo) bool {
    panic("unimplemented")
}
// Hash implements [maphash.Hasher].
func (m *MyHasher) Hash(*maphash.Hash, Foo) {
    panic("unimplemented")
}
Moving declarations across files and packages (preview)
Moving declarations manually by cutting and pasting can easily break references and requires tedious import cleanup across multiple files. While scheduled for an upcoming gopls release, our working implementation already demonstrates how interactive file selection streamlines cross-file and cross-package moves:
- Place your cursor on any top-level declaration and select the “Move declaration X” code action.
- A file picker dialog lets you choose an existing destination .go file or
specify a new file path.
- Gopls moves the declaration along with its dependent declarations (such as unexported helpers or methods) while leaving unrelated symbols in place, updates references across your workspace, and cleans up imports in both the source and destination files.
Interactive "Move declaration" in VS Code
In the example below, we move the type Foo from package from to package
to. Its method Print and the unexported constant bar, which only Foo
uses, move along with it, while the unrelated function Baz stays behind:
// from/from.go
package from
import (
    "fmt"
    "strings"
)
const bar = "bar"
// Doc comment for Foo
type Foo struct{}
func (f Foo) Print() {
    fmt.Println(bar)
}
func Baz() string {
    return strings.ToUpper("baz")
}
// from/from.go
package from
import "strings"
func Baz() string {
    return strings.ToUpper("baz")
}
// to/to.go
package to
import "fmt"
const bar = "bar"
// Doc comment for Foo
type Foo struct{}
func (f Foo) Print() {
    fmt.Println(bar)
}
Slaying the dragon (gopls v0.24.0)
As a demonstration of multi-step interactive dialogs and a self-contained test
case for client editor implementations, gopls v0.24.0 offers a “Slay the
dragon” code action when you place your cursor on a package-level variable
named dragonSlayer (for example, var dragonSlayer string). Happy hunting!
What’s on the Horizon
Interactive refactoring establishes a foundational capability in gopls, opening up several exciting directions on our roadmap:
- Change signature refactoring (#38028): Adding, removing, or reordering function parameters across a workspace requires input that cannot be deduced from syntax alone, such as the new parameter order or the default argument expression to insert at existing call sites. Interactive forms allow gopls to collect these details before rewriting the declaration and all call sites.
- Interactive conflict resolution: When a code transformation encounters naming collisions, identifier shadowing, or ambiguous references, gopls can ask the user for guidance, such as asking for permission to proceed or offering to rename conflicting symbols on the fly.
- Interactive commands beyond code edits: Because interactivity is modeled at the LSP command layer, it naturally generalizes to non-edit server operations that require user configuration, such as configuring test or benchmark runs with profiling flags (CPU, memory, tracing).
Getting Started and Sharing Feedback
Interactive refactoring is available in gopls v0.24.0
and vscode-go v0.56.0
(with proof-of-concept client integrations also explored for
Neovim and
Emacs).
We would love to hear your thoughts as we continue refining interactive code actions in gopls:
- For general feedback or feature requests, file an issue on the Go issue tracker.
- To read the full technical specification—including the stateless form protocol design and alternative approaches we explored—or to join the discussion with the broader LSP community, check out the LSP Interactive Code Actions design document and the ongoing conversation in microsoft/language-server-protocol#1164.
(Special thanks to Alan Donovan, Alex Putman, Brian Wilkerson, Danny Tuppeny, Hana Kim, Madeline Kalil, Peter Weinberger, and Robert Findley for their insights, discussions, feedback, and collaboration on this work.)
Happy refactoring!
