title: Better HTTP/1 connection reuse
text:
The Go Blog
Better HTTP/1 connection reuse
Take a look at the following function:
func getStatus(url string) (int, error) {
    resp, err := http.Get(url)
    if err != nil {
        return 0, err
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    return resp.StatusCode, nil
}
It sends a GET request to url and returns the HTTP status code.
Using HTTP/1 (GODEBUG=http2client=0), calling this function 100 times against
index.golang.org takes ~710 milliseconds on Go 1.26
on my machine. On Go 1.27, the same program takes ~150 milliseconds.
That is almost 5 times faster! How is such a drastic performance difference possible?
The cost of establishing HTTP connections
To understand the difference, consider what happens on the network when we make an HTTP request.
Go’s net/http package supports HTTP/1.0, HTTP/1.1, and
HTTP/2. All three run over TCP, and usually over TLS when talking to HTTPS
endpoints. Making a request over a new connection looks something like this:
- TCP handshake (1 RTT): the client sends a SYN packet, the server
replies with SYN-ACK, and the client replies with ACK. Because the
client can send the first TLS message alongside that final ACK,
establishing the TCP connection takes 1 round-trip time (RTT).
- TLS handshake (2 RTT): next, a TLS handshake exchanges encryption keys and verifies the server’s identity; using TLS 1.2, this takes 2 RTT.
- HTTP request: with the keys exchanged, HTTP requests can finally be sent after a total of 3 RTT.
These round trips (plus some CPU time spent on TLS handshakes) add up quickly. In cross-region communications, one-way latencies often reach or exceed the 50 ms (100 ms RTT) shown in the diagram above. Compared to the 300 ms spent just setting up the connection, the HTTP request itself can be cheap to serve, taking only a little over 1 RTT when bandwidth is plentiful or the HTTP response is small.
Even in more favorable conditions, opening a new connection can still be expensive. Our opening benchmark queries index.golang.org, which is distributed worldwide and supports TLS 1.3. This means that latency is relatively low, and the TLS handshake can actually finish in just 1 RTT. Even so, the performance difference is still very noticeable.
Connection reuse
To avoid paying this setup cost on every request, HTTP clients and servers try to reuse existing connections across multiple requests when possible. The mechanics of this differ based on the HTTP version:
- HTTP/1.0: while not part of the official specification, clients and
servers often opt into connection reuse by sending a Connection: keep-alive header. Reuse continues until either endpoint omits the header
or sends a Connection: close header.
- HTTP/1.1: connections are persistent by default, and can be reused for
subsequent requests and responses unless either side declares otherwise by
sending a Connection: close header.
- HTTP/2: multiple requests and responses can be multiplexed over a single TCP connection.
When connection reuse fails
In HTTP/1 (both HTTP/1.0 and HTTP/1.1), multiple requests and responses on the
same connection are sent sequentially on the wire. If two GET requests are
sent to index.golang.org over the same TCP
connection, the responses arrive as a single stream of bytes:
As shown in the diagram, net/http.Get reads and parses
the status line and headers from the byte stream to populate
net/http.Response, then returns immediately. The
response body remains unread on the connection and is consumed only as the
caller reads from net/http.Response.Body.
Because responses are sent back-to-back on the same stream,
net/http can only find the start of the next response after
the current response body has been read to the very end (as determined by the
Content-Length or Transfer-Encoding header).
Now look back at our example program, where we never read resp.Body:
func getStatus(url string) (int, error) {
    resp, err := http.Get(url)
    if err != nil {
        return 0, err
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    return resp.StatusCode, nil
}
Through Go 1.26, when resp.Body.Close is called, net/http
sees that there is still an unread response body. Realizing that it cannot reuse
the connection, it abandons the existing connection and creates new connections
for its next requests, causing it to repeatedly incur the cost of establishing
new connections.
(HTTP/2 does not have this problem. Because it multiplexes streams of frames over a single connection rather than sending responses strictly back-to-back, an unread response body on one stream does not block other requests from sharing the connection.)
Where failed connection reuse hurts
This subtlety of HTTP/1 connection reuse can cause silent performance degradation in seemingly innocuous code.
As in our opening example, a client might only care about an API response’s
status code. However, the API endpoint it is talking to might send bodies that
provide more detailed but ultimately unused information, such as {"success": true, "message": "update processed"}. This will unfortunately cause connection
reuse to fail.
Even programs that do read the response body can run into this issue if they
stop just short of the end of the body. For example,
encoding/json.Decoder stops reading as soon as
it sees the closing } of a JSON object. If a server sends a JSON response
terminated with a newline, decoding the JSON object will leave the newline still
unread. The connection cannot be reused for a new request until that newline is
consumed. Thus, a healthy connection might end up being abandoned, even though
it was only a single byte away from being reusable.
The manual solution
The unread body problem has been a long-standing sharp edge. Over the years, many Go developers came up with their own workarounds. Most commonly, this is done by draining the response body prior to closing it:
func getStatus(url string) (int, error) {
    resp, err := http.Get(url)
    if err != nil {
        return 0, err
    }
    drainAndCloseBody(resp.Body)
    return resp.StatusCode, nil
}
func drainAndCloseBody(body io.ReadCloser) {
    io.Copy(io.Discard, body) // Drain the response body before closing it.
    body.Close()
}
While this works for small responses, if the unread body is large, establishing a new TCP connection can be faster than downloading and discarding the rest of the body. A better approach is to cap the number of bytes we are willing to drain:
func drainAndCloseBody(body io.ReadCloser) {
    io.CopyN(io.Discard, body, 256<<10) // Only drain up to 256 KB.
    body.Close()
}
However, a server might send a response body that trickles in slowly, so we also need to cap the time we spend draining:
func drainAndCloseBody(body io.ReadCloser) {
    drainDone := make(chan struct{}, 1)
    go func() {
        io.CopyN(io.Discard, body, 256<<10) // Only drain up to 256 KB.
        drainDone <- struct{}{}
    }()
    // Only spend at most 50 ms trying to drain the response body.
    select {
    case <-drainDone:
    case <-time.After(50 * time.Millisecond):
        // If we reach the 50 ms timeout, body.Close will run and interrupt the
        // io.CopyN, preventing goroutine leaks.
    }
    body.Close()
}
Of course, we also do not want to block for up to 50 milliseconds when closing a response body. Instead, we can drain the body asynchronously in the background and let it race against subsequent requests:
func drainAndCloseBody(body io.ReadCloser) {
    drainDone := make(chan struct{}, 1)
    go func() {
        io.CopyN(io.Discard, body, 256<<10) // Only drain up to 256 KB.
        drainDone <- struct{}{}
    }()
    go func() {
        // Only spend at most 50 ms trying to drain the response body.
        select {
        case <-drainDone:
            // If the drain can finish before a new request is sent, the
            // connection will be reused; otherwise, a new connection is
            // created, and the current connection will be put in a pool of
            // idle connections, potentially being reused for another future
            // request.
        case <-time.After(50 * time.Millisecond):
            // If we reach the 50 ms timeout, body.Close will run and interrupt
            // the io.CopyN, preventing goroutine leaks.
        }
        body.Close()
    }()
}
As we can see, draining response bodies safely is surprisingly tricky and cumbersome. Worse, as the practice of draining response bodies spread, some nuances were often lost. This has led to misunderstandings such as attempting to drain response bodies for HTTP/2 connections, when doing so is unnecessary.
The current state and conclusion
Starting in Go 1.27, net/http.Transport
automatically does everything we have implemented in the code above: it will
asynchronously drain an unread HTTP/1 response body for up to 50 ms or 256 KB.
It also implements additional optimizations; for example, when a response
contains the Connection: close header, draining the body is guaranteed to be
wasted work, and it therefore skips doing so. Note that this behavior might
evolve in future versions of Go, as other possible enhancements become apparent.
As a general best practice, we now recommend that users simply close their HTTP bodies once they no longer need them, like in our original example:
func getStatus(url string) (int, error) {
    resp, err := http.Get(url)
    if err != nil {
        return 0, err
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    return resp.StatusCode, nil
}
Go is all about simplicity. Let your code stay clean and simple, and let
net/http deal with the complexities on your behalf.

title: Arch-specific SIMD in Go
text:
The Go Blog
Arch-specific SIMD in Go
Since Go 1.26, we have supported an experimental amd64 SIMD API. Now in Go 1.27, we support two more architectures: arm64 and wasm.
The new APIs can be accessed by setting GOEXPERIMENT=simd when building a program. They are defined in the simd/archsimd package.
archsimd is the lower-level infrastructure that simd builds on, essentially the intrinsics layer in other languages. For exotic operations that only exist on a specific architecture, users can access them by transitioning from simd to archsimd (via ToArch and <Types>FromArch). For details, please refer to the simd blog post.
For readers with prior knowledge of SIMD intrinsics in other languages, you might find that our archsimd API does not directly mirror the underlying hardware instructions:
- We give our APIs sensible names: e.g., instead of _mm512_slli_epi64, we just call it ShiftAllLeft.
- We leave some architecture details to compiler optimizations rather than exposing them in the API: e.g., instead of _mm512_maskz_add_ps(m, x, y), we optimize x.Add(y).Masked(m) into the same instruction.
These design decisions make our APIs smaller and more accessible, and they also happily make the simd implementation much easier.
For readers without prior knowledge of SIMD intrinsics, we hope our low-level API is a natural and pleasant journey for you.
Please share your feedback and comments. Anything about usability, performance, etc., is appreciated. The parent issue for this project is #73787.
What is SIMD
SIMD stands for Single Instruction, Multiple Data. SIMD instructions operate on wide registers (128-bit, 256-bit, or more) containing multiple 8- to 64-bit elements, performing operations across all elements in parallel. Wider registers and parallel execution provide a significant performance boost to algorithms that can take advantage of them.
Until now, anyone who wanted to use SIMD in Go had to endure the friction of writing assembly language. The new archsimd package is here to change that.
Goals
The goal is to support as many SIMD instructions across different architectures as possible. Currently, we have amd64, arm64, and wasm available. Our amd64 support has the largest API surface, covering AVX, AVX2, and many AVX-512 extensions. Our arm64 support currently covers NEON, with SVE and some SVE2 already on the way. Our wasm support is also mostly complete, thanks to its well-defined 128-bit SIMD abstraction.
Some users might be interested in matrix extensions on certain architectures, such as AMX and SME. We haven’t fully settled on how to represent matrices effectively in Go, so they are not yet supported, but we might support them in the future.
API Design and Naming
Types
The architecture-specific SIMD API is imported from simd/archsimd. archsimd uses distinct struct types, such as Float32x4, Int32x8, or Uint8x16, to signal the shape and element type of each vector, and defines operations as methods on those types. At this moment, archsimd supports only fixed-width vector extensions. Scalable vector extensions like arm64 SVE and RVV will have different struct types to represent vectors. Mask types also come with vector-like shapes, e.g., Mask32x4.
Methods
Across different vector widths, element types, and architectures, we use the same method name whenever operations are semantically identical:
- Regardless of vector width or architecture, element-wise addition is simply x.Add(y); the type of x determines which instruction to emit. Instead of 18 different function names for addition, there is only one method name.
- When instructions on different architectures look similar at a glance but differ in edge-case behavior, we give them distinct names so differences don’t silently bite you. For example, 16-byte table lookup on amd64 (VPSHUFB) zeros the output byte when the index is negative (index < 0) and wraps modulo 16 otherwise, so we call it PermuteOrZero. On arm64 NEON (VTBL) and wasm (i8x16.swizzle), any out-of-range index (index < 0 || index >= 16) zeros the output byte, so we call it LookupOrZero.
- On amd64, many 256-bit and 512-bit instructions operate independently within 128-bit lanes rather than across the entire register. We explicitly suffix those methods with Grouped (such as InterleaveLoGrouped or PermuteOrZeroGrouped) to make the 128-bit lane boundary obvious.
Methods require a receiver value, which doesn’t work for creating a vector from memory or a scalar. For those, archsimd provides package-level functions named with the target vector type:
- Slices (the default): In Go 1.27, loading and storing slices use the shortest names: archsimd.LoadFloat32x4(s []float32) Float32x4 and x.Store(s []float32). For tail elements that may be shorter than a full vector, archsimd.LoadFloat32x4Part(s []float32) (Float32x4, int) zero-fills the remaining lanes and returns the number of elements loaded, paired with x.StorePart(s []float32) int.
- Arrays and Broadcasts: Fixed-size array pointers use the Array suffix (archsimd.LoadFloat32x4Array(y *[4]float32) and x.StoreArray(y *[4]float32)), and archsimd.BroadcastFloat32x4(v float32) broadcasts a scalar to all lanes.
Type Reinterpretation
Reinterpretations are type casts without any cost. SIMD algorithms frequently reinterpret bits across element types and widths.
In the Go 1.26 experiment, we implemented this with As<Type> methods, which suffered from a quadratic explosion of type pairs and couldn’t generalize to width-agnostic vectors in simd or SVE.
In Go 1.27, we replace them with composable zero-cost conversions:
- ToBits() reinterprets a signed integer or float vector as an unsigned integer vector of the same element width (e.g., Int32x4.ToBits() -> Uint32x4), and BitsToInt32() / BitsToFloat32() converts back.
- ReshapeToUint<W>s() on unsigned vectors changes the element width within the same register width. For example, if x is an archsimd.Uint8x16, then x.ReshapeToUint32s().BitsToFloat32() reinterprets the bits of x as an archsimd.Float32x4 at zero runtime cost.
Masks
Different architectures encode vector masks very differently, e.g. k mask registers on AVX-512, full vector bitmasks on AVX/AVX2, NEON, and wasm, and predicate registers on SVE. To hide this hardware detail, archsimd provides opaque Mask types (such as Mask32x4) matching each vector shape:
- Comparisons like x.Greater(y) produce a Mask.
- x.Masked(m) zeros elements where m is false, and x.IfElse(m, y) (which replaces Merge from Go 1.26) selects elements from x where m is true and from y where m is false.
- The compiler peepholes mask operations with the surrounding instructions: on AVX-512, x.Add(y).Masked(m) or x.Add(y).IfElse(m, z) compiles into a single zero-masked or merge-masked VPADD instruction; on AVX2, NEON, or wasm, it lowers to the appropriate bitwise AND or blend/bitselect instruction.
Examples
Portable algorithms like inner product can easily be implemented using the portable simd package, as shown in the companion simd blog post. However, we still expose archsimd to tap into exotic, architecture-specific instructions that do not fit into a portable intersection API, or instructions that can simply do things faster than what simd provides.
On amd64, the GFNI extension exposes GaloisFieldAffineTransform operations. Putting aside what a Galois Field is, these operations do a simple thing:
// Each element of A is interpreted as a matrix of 8 rows of vectors of 8 bits.
// Each element of x is interpreted as a vector of 8 bits.
// The b argument is likewise a vector of 8 bits.
// The result is z[i] = (A[i/8] * x[i]) + b.
//
// The matrix * and vector + follow the usual rules for linear algebra,
// but based on AND and XOR for scalar * and +
//
// Asm: VGF2P8AFFINEQB, CPU Feature: AVX512GFNI
func (x Uint8x16) GaloisFieldAffineTransform(A Uint64x2, b uint8) Uint8x16
Each 8x8 bit matrix A is packed row-by-row into a single uint64. Because any linear combination or permutation of the 8 bits within a byte can be written as an 8x8 bit matrix, this single instruction is a Swiss Army knife for byte-level bit manipulation.
For example, reversing the bit order of every byte (bits.Reverse8) normally requires nibble lookup tables, masks, shifts, and ORs in SIMD. With GaloisFieldAffineTransform, we can simply multiply each byte by the 8x8 anti-diagonal identity matrix (0x8040201008040201) to reverse all 8 bits of 64 bytes at a time in a single instruction:
/*
    Anti-diagonal 8x8 bit matrix (0x8040201008040201):
    [ 0 0 0 0 0 0 0 1 ]   [ x7 ]   [ x0 ]
    [ 0 0 0 0 0 0 1 0 ]   [ x6 ]   [ x1 ]
    [ 0 0 0 0 0 1 0 0 ]   [ x5 ]   [ x2 ]
    [ 0 0 0 0 1 0 0 0 ] * [ x4 ] = [ x3 ]
    [ 0 0 0 1 0 0 0 0 ]   [ x3 ]   [ x4 ]
    [ 0 0 1 0 0 0 0 0 ]   [ x2 ]   [ x5 ]
    [ 0 1 0 0 0 0 0 0 ]   [ x1 ]   [ x6 ]
    [ 1 0 0 0 0 0 0 0 ]   [ x0 ]   [ x7 ]
*/
func ReverseBits(dst, src []uint8) {
    if !archsimd.X86.AVX512GFNI() {
        // A slow fallback emulation impl, details omitted.
        slowReverseBits(dst, src)
        return
    }
    if len(src) > len(dst) {
        // Make sure src and dst are the same size
        src = src[:len(dst)]
    }
    revMatrix := archsimd.BroadcastUint64x8(0x8040201008040201)
    var v archsimd.Uint8x64
    var i int
    for i = 0; i < len(src)-v.Len()+1; i += v.Len() {
        v = archsimd.LoadUint8x64(src[i : i+v.Len()])
        v.GaloisFieldAffineTransform(revMatrix, 0).Store(dst[i : i+v.Len()])
    }
    if i < len(src) {
        v, _ = archsimd.LoadUint8x64Part(src[i:])
        v.GaloisFieldAffineTransform(revMatrix, 0).StorePart(dst[i:])
    }
}
Another example is matrix transpose. On amd64, the permutation instructions are shaped in a non-portable way, so using simd is cumbersome and might incur emulations. An efficient implementation can be written more directly in archsimd. The example below transposes an 8-by-8 matrix of 32-bit integers in registers on amd64 using AVX2’s 128-bit lane-grouped interleaves (InterleaveLoGrouped, InterleaveHiGrouped) and cross-lane permutations (ConcatPermuteScalarsGrouped, ConcatPermute128Scalars):
func Transpose8(a0, a1, a2, a3, a4, a5, a6, a7 archsimd.Int32x8) (
    b0, b1, b2, b3, b4, b5, b6, b7 archsimd.Int32x8) {
    if !archsimd.X86.AVX2() {
        // A slow fallback emulation impl, details omitted.
        return slowTranspose8(a0, a1, a2, a3, a4, a5, a6, a7)
    }
    /*
            LOW  HIGH
        a0: abcd efgh
        a1: ijkl mnop
        a2: qrst uvwx
        a3: 0123 4567
        a4: ABCD EFGH
        a5: IJKL MNOP
        a6: QRST UVWX
        a7: 89yz YZ$@
    */
    t0 := a0.InterleaveLoGrouped(a1) // t0 = aibj emfn
    t1 := a0.InterleaveHiGrouped(a1) // t1 = ckdl gohp
    t2 := a2.InterleaveLoGrouped(a3) // t2 = q0r1 u4v5
    t3 := a2.InterleaveHiGrouped(a3) // t3 = s2t3 w6x7
    t4 := a4.InterleaveLoGrouped(a5) // t4 = AIBJ EMFN
    t5 := a4.InterleaveHiGrouped(a5) // t5 = CKDL GOHP
    t6 := a6.InterleaveLoGrouped(a7) // t6 = Q8R9 UYVZ
    t7 := a6.InterleaveHiGrouped(a7) // t7 = SyTz W$X@
    a0 = t0.ConcatPermuteScalarsGrouped(0, 1, 4, 5, t2) // a0 = aiq0 emu4
    a1 = t0.ConcatPermuteScalarsGrouped(2, 3, 6, 7, t2) // a1 = bjr1 fnv5
    a2 = t1.ConcatPermuteScalarsGrouped(0, 1, 4, 5, t3) // a2 = cks2 gow6
    a3 = t1.ConcatPermuteScalarsGrouped(2, 3, 6, 7, t3) // a3 = dlt3 hpx7
    a4 = t4.ConcatPermuteScalarsGrouped(0, 1, 4, 5, t6) // a4 = AIQ8 EMUY
    a5 = t4.ConcatPermuteScalarsGrouped(2, 3, 6, 7, t6) // a5 = BJR9 FNVZ
    a6 = t5.ConcatPermuteScalarsGrouped(0, 1, 4, 5, t7) // a6 = CKSy GOW$
    a7 = t5.ConcatPermuteScalarsGrouped(2, 3, 6, 7, t7) // a7 = DLTz HPX@
    b0 = a0.ConcatPermute128Scalars(0, 2, a4) // b0 = aiq0 AIQ8
    b1 = a1.ConcatPermute128Scalars(0, 2, a5) // b1 = bjr1 BJR9
    b2 = a2.ConcatPermute128Scalars(0, 2, a6) // b2 = cks2 CKSy
    b3 = a3.ConcatPermute128Scalars(0, 2, a7) // b3 = dlt3 DLTz
    b4 = a0.ConcatPermute128Scalars(1, 3, a4) // b4 = emu4 EMUY
    b5 = a1.ConcatPermute128Scalars(1, 3, a5) // b5 = fnv5 FNVZ
    b6 = a2.ConcatPermute128Scalars(1, 3, a6) // b6 = gow6 GOW$
    b7 = a3.ConcatPermute128Scalars(1, 3, a7) // b7 = hpx7 HPX@
    return
}
Good Practices
When walking through the examples above, you might have a few questions:
- What is archsimd.X86.AVX512GFNI(), and can I omit it?
- Why is the strided loop written as i = 0; i < len(src)-v.Len()+1; i += v.Len(), instead of i = 0; i + v.Len() <= len(src); i += v.Len()?
- Why does Transpose8 take 8 vector parameters rather than a struct or an [8]archsimd.Int32x8 array?
At first glance these choices might look like minor stylistic preferences, but each of them is chosen for an important performance or correctness reason:
- CPU feature checks (archsimd.X86.*, archsimd.ARM64.*)
On amd64, we provide runtime feature checks like archsimd.X86.AVX(), AVX2(), AVX512(), and extension checks like AVX512GFNI() or AVX512VNNI(); on arm64, NEON is always available, and we provide checks for optional extensions like archsimd.ARM64.PMULL(), SVE(), and SVE2(). The compiler doesn’t know ahead of time whether the machine running your binary supports optional SIMD extensions. If you don’t guard your SIMD code with the appropriate feature check, your program may crash with SIGILL on hardware that lacks the instruction.
Just as importantly, CPU feature checks act as compiler optimization hints. For example, AVX-512 supports hardware merge-masking on instruction outputs. How the compiler lowers x.Add(y).IfElse(m, z) on a 128-bit or 256-bit vector depends on which CPU features are known to be available. If the code is not guarded by archsimd.X86.AVX512(), the compiler must conservatively emit a vector VPADD followed by a VPBLEND instruction. Inside an if archsimd.X86.AVX512() block, however, the compiler knows AVX-512 is available and fuses the sequence into a single merge-masked AVX-512 VPADD instruction.
- Bounds check elimination in strided loops How you write the loop bound determines whether the compiler’s prove pass can eliminate slice bounds checks inside the loop. In i + v.Len() <= len(src), the addition i + v.Len() could theoretically overflow to a negative int if len(src) were near math.MaxInt, which prevents the compiler from proving that i is always non-negative and in-bounds. Writing i < len(src)-v.Len()+1 avoids that potential overflow, allowing the loop body to compile with zero bounds checks.
- Keeping vectors in registers (avoiding large composite types) Transpose8 passes 8 vector parameters rather than a struct of 8 fields or an [8]archsimd.Int32x8 array because Go’s ABI and SSA backend currently place large composite types in memory rather than in registers (a known issue tracked at #24416). Because SIMD vectors are 16 to 64 bytes each, spilling them to the stack hurts performance much more than spilling scalar values. This applies to both function parameters and local variables, so avoid wrapping SIMD vectors inside large arrays or structs in hot loops. There are ongoing efforts to promote composite memory accesses back into registers, which have not yet landed in Go 1.27.
Trying it out
In Go 1.27, GOEXPERIMENT=simd supports amd64 (AVX, AVX2, and AVX-512), arm64 (NEON), and wasm (WebAssembly 128-bit SIMD) out of the box. Whether you are on an Intel/AMD machine, an arm64 server or Apple Silicon Mac (M1/M2/M3/M4), or targeting WebAssembly, you can try archsimd natively right away:
GOEXPERIMENT=simd go test simd/archsimd/...
You can also cross-test wasm (or amd64 via Rosetta emulation on Apple Silicon) by setting GOARCH:
# Run wasm SIMD tests using a WASI runtime:
GOOS=wasip1 GOARCH=wasm GOEXPERIMENT=simd go test simd/archsimd/...
# Or run amd64 AVX2 tests on Apple Silicon via Rosetta:
GOARCH=amd64 GOEXPERIMENT=simd go test simd/archsimd/...
We’re interested in all sorts of feedback! Early users have already helped us catch bugs (such as #77582) and identify places where code generation or API ergonomics could be improved. We tried hard to pick clear, consistent names and cover the most useful instructions, but archsimd is a massive API surface and there is always room to improve.
Future work
For Go 1.28 and beyond, we are actively working on completing arm64 SVE and SVE2 support in archsimd (introducing width-agnostic scalable vector types like archsimd.Float32s backed directly by hardware SVE registers and predicates) and wiring it into simd. We also plan to expand archsimd to additional architectures such as riscv64, ppc64, s390x, and loong64, improve register promotion for composite types, and continue filling in instructions and compiler optimizations based on community feedback.

title: Platform-independent SIMD in Go
text:
The Go Blog
Platform-independent SIMD in Go
Go 1.26 and 1.27 include experimental APIs for Single Instruction Multiple Data (SIMD) operations. SIMD is a native feature of many modern CPUs that allows software to perform uniform operations across vectors of data very quickly, such as adding 8 pairs of float64 values in a single instruction. It can significantly speed up many computationally-intensive tasks, ranging from cryptography to data processing to AI. In fact, Go’s Green Tea garbage collector even makes use of SIMD to accelerate scanning memory for live objects.
Prior to these new experimental APIs, the only way to access this functionality from Go was by writing Go assembly. This was only worth it for truly performance-critical compute kernels, which meant plenty of software that could benefit from SIMD simply left a lot of the CPU unused.
Go 1.26 introduced a SIMD API for amd64, and Go 1.27 added APIs for arm64 (specifically NEON) and wasm. However, a basic challenge for a SIMD API is the enormous variation between platforms, not simply in what operations they support, but even in how vectors are represented. Some platforms provide fixed-size vectors, typically between 128 bits and 512 bits, while on others the vector size isn’t known at build time and must be queried when the program starts. To provide full access to the breadth of these platforms, these APIs live in an architecture-dependent archsimd package.
But Go 1.27 goes beyond these architecture-dependent APIs and introduces an experimental, fully portable, platform- and size-agnostic SIMD interface,
loosely based on Highway for C++.  The goal is to support write-once near-asm-performance “simd” code on platforms with SIMD support, and to provide a competent emulation on those platforms that do not (yet) have SIMD support.  The simd package currently supports AVX, AVX2, and AVX512 on amd64, NEON on arm64, and wasm’s SIMD instructions.
Motivation: variation among SIMD architectures
SIMD architectures vary in several dimensions. Some provide a single fixed vector size (wasm, PowerPC, and s390x, 128 bits). Some provide several fixed vector sizes (amd64, with 128, 256, and 512; loong64 with 128 and 256). Riscv64 supports vectors of unspecified size between 128 and 65536 bits, though the length is limited to powers of 2. Arm64 supports one fixed size (128 bits, NEON), and one variable size (128-2048 bits, powers of two only, SVE). On a given instance of a particular architecture, determining what sizes that particular instance happens to support requires feature checks: amd64, but is it AVX, AVX2, or AVX512? Arm64, but is it NEON or SVE? If SVE, how large? Which variant of SVE: SVE, SVE2, or SVE2.1?
Different SIMD architectures vary in how they handle vector masking. For vectors, if-then-else across a vector can be implemented with masks; do the operation, but only assign the result (or load, or store) where the mask is “true”. Some SIMD variants do not provide masks; all operations work across all elements, and “masking” is done with vector bitmasks and vector boolean operations (wasm, AVX, AVX2, NEON). Some provide special mask registers, with one bit governing operations on one vector element (AVX512 and RVV). Others (SVE) allocate one bit per vector byte, but the least-significant bit of each element’s mask bits governs masked operations. AVX2 also supports masked loads and stores, but using a plain vector as the mask, and with the most-significant bit governing the operation.
A third source of variation is in the operations themselves. Each architecture provides its own primitives for rearranging vector elements; some require constant inputs, others support variable inputs. Different SIMD architectures support different crypto-related operations. Even basic arithmetic can have varying support; for example wasm lacks comparisons for vectors of 64-bit integers. Even for a given vector length on a particular architecture, instruction support depends on “features” that must be checked.
Even though Go’s architecture-dependent archsimd package was designed to be as uniform as possible across architectures, many of these quirks remain, and make designing, writing, and testing code for multiplatform SIMD onerous.  We could do more in the archsimd package to make the different architectures appear more similar, but we can only go so far without compromising efficiency.
Overview
The new simd package hides these differences by removing fixed-size vectors from the type system, and by only supporting those operations that are in the intersection of all the different platforms, and fills gaps in the intersection with efficient emulation in terms of other SIMD instructions.  The goal is a set of operations that is
- adequate to support many data processing algorithms that benefit from a vectorized implementation (but are not tied to a particular vector size),
- is as efficient as assembly language when the source code operations match the underlying hardware,
- is otherwise emulated as well as possible,
- and is easy to read and understand (even/especially if an LLM ends up writing the code).
On platforms that lack SIMD instructions or that lack support in archsimd, all of the operations are emulated,
so that code written using the simd package will always run.
To use this experimental package, set GOEXPERIMENT=simd at build time, just like using the experimental archsimd package.
The simd vector types are just capitalized, plural, primitive types, for example simd.Uint8s or simd.Float32s. Vectors are loaded from and stored to slices, for example:
// innerProduct returns the inner product of x and y.
func innerProduct(x, y []float32) float32 {
    var a simd.Float32s
    var i int
    for i = 0; i < len(x)-a.Len()+1; i += a.Len() {
        u := simd.LoadFloat32s(x[i : i+a.Len()])
        v := simd.LoadFloat32s(y[i : i+a.Len()])
        a = u.MulAdd(v, a)
    }
    if i < len(x) {
        u, _ := simd.LoadFloat32sPart(x[i:])
        v, _ := simd.LoadFloat32sPart(y[i:])
        a = u.MulAdd(v, a)
    }
    return sum(a)
}
// sum returns scalar sum of elements of x.
func sum(x simd.Float32s) float32 {
    s := make([]float32, x.Len())
    x.Store(s)
    var r float32
    for _, e := range s {
        r += e
    }
    return r
}
This example also shows one of the limitations of the first experimental release of this package; because there’s no common way to sum across all the elements of a vector, it’s not supported by simd in Go 1.27, though ReduceSum will appear in the next release so sum can be replaced with just simd.ReduceSum.
SIMD comparisons produce mask values, which are specific to the corresponding vector element width, so that comparisons of Int8s produce Mask8s, etc., and mask values can be used to select and filter vectors.

Transition to/from platform-specific code
It may happen that the simd package is too limited for all parts of a particular application, or that we have not yet provided an adequate emulation for some necessary feature.  For that case, the simd package supports transition to and from architecture-specific SIMD.  Each vector type in the simd package has a conversion method ToArch() returning an any.  That any can be type-asserted to one of the architecture-specific types for a platform.  To convert back, use one of the simd.<SimdType>FromArch functions.  For portable code this creates an obligation to write architecture-specific code for each of the platforms, including an emulation.
Here’s a complete example for a method/function that is currently missing, but should be added in Go 1.28. Suppose your algorithm needs Int8s.OnesCount() (which simd in Go 1.27 lacks).  Rather than rewriting the entire algorithm for each platform, it’s possible to just implement the missing operation.
First, for amd64, which lacks the instruction for AVX and AVX2, but not AVX512:
//go:build goexperiment.simd && amd64
package simd_test
import (
    "simd"
    "simd/archsimd"
)
var popcnt4x16 = [16]int8{0, 1, 1, 2, 1, 2, 2, 3, 1, 2, 2, 3, 2, 3, 3, 4}
var popcnt4x32 = [32]int8{
    0, 1, 1, 2, 1, 2, 2, 3, 1, 2, 2, 3, 2, 3, 3, 4,
    0, 1, 1, 2, 1, 2, 2, 3, 1, 2, 2, 3, 2, 3, 3, 4,
}
// OnesCount returns the number of one bits for each element.
func OnesCount(v simd.Int8s) simd.Int8s {
    switch x := v.ToArch().(type) {
    case archsimd.Int8x16:
        lut := archsimd.LoadInt8x16Array(&popcnt4x16)
        mask0f := archsimd.BroadcastInt8x16(0x0f)
        lo := x.And(mask0f)
        hi := x.ToBits().ReshapeToUint16s().ShiftAllRight(4).
                ReshapeToUint8s().BitsToInt8().And(mask0f)
        return simd.Int8sFromArch(lut.PermuteOrZero(lo).
                Add(lut.PermuteOrZero(hi)))
    case archsimd.Int8x32:
        lut := archsimd.LoadInt8x32Array(&popcnt4x32)
        mask0f := archsimd.BroadcastInt8x32(0x0f)
        lo := x.And(mask0f)
        hi := x.ToBits().ReshapeToUint16s().ShiftAllRight(4).
                ReshapeToUint8s().BitsToInt8().And(mask0f)
        return simd.Int8sFromArch(lut.PermuteOrZeroGrouped(lo).
                Add(lut.PermuteOrZeroGrouped(hi)))
    case archsimd.Int8x64:
        return simd.Int8sFromArch(x.OnesCount())
    default:
        // GODEBUG=simd=0 emulation
        return OnesCountEmulated(v)
    }
}
The interface conversion and type switch look like they should be inefficient, but the compiler-side implementation of simd specializes code and optimizes away the type switch.
NEON and Wasm both support Int8s.OnesCount(), so their implementation is much simpler, though it still uses Int8s.ToArch and Int8sFromArch.
//go:build goexperiment.simd && (wasm || arm64)
package simd_test
import (
    "simd"
    "simd/archsimd"
)
// OnesCount returns the number of one bits for each element.
func OnesCount(v simd.Int8s) simd.Int8s {
    // TODO when SVE is added, this won't work
    switch x := v.ToArch().(type) {
    case archsimd.Int8x16:
        return simd.Int8sFromArch(x.OnesCount())
    default:
        // GODEBUG=simd=0 emulation
        return OnesCountEmulated(v)
    }
}
Don’t forget that some people don’t have hardware SIMD support:
//go:build goexperiment.simd && !(amd64 || wasm || arm64)
package simd_test
import (
    "simd"
)
// OnesCount returns the number of one bits for each element.
func OnesCount(v simd.Int8s) simd.Int8s {
    return OnesCountEmulated(v)
}
And to complete the exercise, a separate emulation function shared as a fallback across all implementations:
//go:build goexperiment.simd
package simd_test
import (
    "simd"
)
// OnesCountEmulated returns the number of one bits for each element.
func OnesCountEmulated(v simd.Int8s) simd.Int8s {
    a := [2]uint64{}
    v.ToBits().ReshapeToUint64s().Store(a[:])
    a0, a1 := a[0], a[1]
    m1 := uint64(0x5555555555555555)
    m2 := uint64(0x3333333333333333)
    m4 := uint64(0x0f0f0f0f0f0f0f0f)
    a0 = (a0 & m1) + ((a0 >> 1) & m1)
    a1 = (a1 & m1) + ((a1 >> 1) & m1)
    a0 = (a0 & m2) + ((a0 >> 2) & m2)
    a1 = (a1 & m2) + ((a1 >> 2) & m2)
    a0 = (a0 & m4) + ((a0 >> 4) & m4)
    a1 = (a1 & m4) + ((a1 >> 4) & m4)
    a[0], a[1] = a0, a1
    return simd.LoadUint64s(a[:]).ReshapeToUint8s().BitsToInt8()
}
API intersection and method emulation
Whatever operations the simd package offers need to run acceptably well on most architectures.  As a first step, any operation that is supported everywhere, can easily be supported on simd.  This tends to include loads, stores, arithmetic, and comparisons (but not all comparisons!).
A naive intersection across SIMD methods from different architectures still leaves plenty of holes.
These are filled by adding emulations to the various architecture-specific archsimd APIs.
These APIs already contain many trivial emulations to simplify life for Go programmers;
signed and unsigned integer addition use the same instruction,
but in the same way that Go supports the + operator for both int and uint,
the archsimd package provides both Int8x16.Add(Int8x16) and Uint8x16.Add(Uint8x16),
even though those compile to the same instruction.
Modern programming languages also don’t expect programmers to know how to implement floating point negation and absolute value with bit fiddling,
so archsimd implements that where necessary, or “emulates” if you look at it just so.
There are many emulations that require just 2 or 3 instructions; for example, some architectures support only a same-value shift distance across vector elements, while others support a different shift distance for each vector element.  To support scalar shifting in simd, we emulate scalar shift with vector shift.  Some architectures lack some unsigned comparisons–these are just signed comparison, plus two XORs with a constant.
Not all missing instructions are that simple.  The “carryless multiply” instruction is important to cryptography and CRC checksumming, but it isn’t always supported.  Leaving that out of the simd API would prevent its use for some important algorithms.  Therefore, we provide an emulation, and because one important use is in crypto, its run time does not vary depending on its inputs.
In other cases, rather than implement a primitive instruction like “add pairs” (also called “horizontal addition”), for the simd package in the next release we will provide the higher level operation that add pairs is usually used for, which is sum reduction.  This also helps insulate users from vector-length dependence; even given the hardware instruction for adding pairs, the number of reduction steps depends on the vector length.
The constraint of supporting all platforms, including ones that we predict will appear in archsimd within the next year or so, forces a somewhat conservative approach to which methods we add to simd.  Riscv64, ppc64, s390x, and loong64 all have their own SIMD extensions.
GODEBUG settings
On platforms where there is some hardware support, behavior can be modified with GODEBUG, to make it easier to test simd-using code with various hardware configurations. You can set the GODEBUG environment variable prior to executing your program.
In Go 1.27, levels of SIMD support are roughly described by vector length:
- GODEBUG=simd=0 means use emulation for SIMD operations even if the hardware support is available.
- GODEBUG=simd=128 means use 128-bit vectors and their features.  If the features aren’t available, panic immediately.
- GODEBUG=simd=256 means use 256-bit vectors and their features, if possible.
- GODEBUG=simd=512 means use 512-bit vectors and their features, if possible.
- GODEBUG=simd=+128 means use 128-bit vectors and their features even if some features are not supported. If unsupported instructions are used, the code will panic, but if they are not it may still run.  An example of this is Raspberry Pi, which supports NEON but lacks PMULL (carryless multiply).
- GODEBUG=simd=+256 means use 256-bit vectors and their features even if some features are not supported. If unsupported instructions are used, the code will panic, but if they are not it may still run.  An example of this is Apple Silicon’s amd64 emulation, which supports AVX2 but not VPCLMULQDQ (again, carryless multiply).
- GODEBUG=simd=+512 means use 512-bit vectors, even if some features are not supported.
Implementation details
If you are debugging code that uses simd, or even just look at a stack trace, you will notice some weird extra types and methods.  The reason is that simd is both a package, an internal implementation package, and some AST rewriting in the front end of the compiler.
The AST rewrite creates multiple specialized copies of functions, variables, and types that mention simd types, where simd types are replaced with references to size-specialized types in simd/internal/bridge.  Each of these bridge types is defined as an archsimd type, but with a restricted set of methods.  The specialized functions, variables, and types acquire a suffix of the form @simdNNN, where NNN is either a vector length (128, 256, or 512) or 0, indicating emulation.  Functions that mention simd internally, but not in their signature, are converted to wrappers that switch on the SIMD level detected at program start, and call the appropriate specialized version of that function.  Specialized functions call other specialized functions directly without dispatch overhead (and perhaps with inlining).  This rewrite strategy was chosen as a compromise between code duplication and SIMD performance; the overhead is hoisted as high as necessary to avoid dispatch within SIMD computations, but not higher.  If SIMD dispatch appears “too low” in a computation, a gratuitous mention of a simd type will move it upwards, as in this example:
func BenchmarkVpsumdSIMD(b *testing.B) {
    // mention "simd" so the benchmark loop calls specialized vpsumd3 directly
    var _ simd.Uint64s
    var w, x, y, z uint64 = ... // magic constants omitted.
    var lo, hi uint64
    for b.Loop() {
        // vpsumd3 does simd stuff, but lacks a simd signature,
        // so that it can be compared with non-SIMD emulations.
        lo, hi = vpsumd3(w, x, y, z)
    }
    sinkLo, sinkHi = lo, hi
}
What’s coming
We plan to publish a blog post describing archsimd in greater detail soon.
For Go 1.28, we intend to add SVE support to archsimd, and also hope to add that to simd.  More importantly, we hope to add additional SIMD operations to those that the simd package already supports (e.g., OnesCount, mask operations, reduction operations, vector shuffling operations). Go 1.28 will also include a small number of “feature variants” to avoid downgrading all the way to full emulation for platforms that have a hardware vector implementation but just lack one or a few operations, such as Raspberry Pi.

title: Size-Specialized Memory Allocation
text:
The Go Blog
Size-Specialized Memory Allocation
Go 1.27 includes faster memory allocation for allocations of 80 bytes or fewer. Allocations can be up to 20-30% faster, making allocation-heavy programs up to 1% faster. The Go runtime improves the performance of those allocations by adding specialized functions that are used to allocate certain sizes. These specialized functions can then make certain assumptions that make them faster and easier to optimize. This blog post will explain how this works and how it makes your programs faster.
Heap allocations are created by the runtime’s mallocgc function, which requires the size
of the allocation and whether it contains pointers. When the compiler determines that an
object escapes to the heap or otherwise needs to be dynamically
allocated, it inserts a call to newobject, which is a simple wrapper function that extracts
the size of the object and whether it contains pointers and passes those to mallocgc.
These two pieces of information determine most of the work that the allocator needs to do. The size is important because the allocator defines ranges of sizes called “size classes”. For most allocations that are not too large and not too small, it will return a block of memory from a list of free objects that are all sized to the maximum size of the size class. So, for instance, size class 3 is 17-24 bytes. So whether you allocate 17 bytes or 24 bytes, the allocator will give you the next free 24 byte object available in its list of 24 byte objects. Below is a table of the size ranges of each of the size classes up to 80 bytes. There are separate sets of free lists, which we call spans, depending on whether the allocation has pointers, because of the bookkeeping we need to do for the garbage collector.
| Size class | Range of sizes | 
|---|---|
| 1 | 1-8 bytes | 
| 2 | 9-16 bytes | 
| 3 | 17-24 bytes | 
| 4 | 25-32 bytes | 
| 5 | 33-48 bytes | 
| 6 | 49-64 bytes | 
| 7 | 65-80 bytes | 
Because the size class and whether the allocation contains pointers determine which span
we allocate from, the allocator has a type called the span class, whose value encodes both:
it’s defined as sizeClass<<1 | noPointers. When implementing size-specialized malloc
it was clear that it made the most sense to specialize on these span classes because much of
the behavior of the allocator was determined by the span class.
We generate a specialized mallocgc variant for every span class. For instance, the function
that allocates pointer-free objects in size class 3 is called mallocgcSmallNoScanSC3.
Small means not tiny or large, NoScan means it has no pointers, and SC3 means size class 3
(17-24 bytes). Specialized functions are designed to be as simple as possible and cannot handle
every corner case during allocation. When they detect such a case, such as when the GC is active,
they fall back to a more generic allocation routine.
So we end up with a new specialized mallocgc function for the tiny case (always no pointers)
and one for each non-tiny span class: the non-pointer spans of size class 2 and above, and
the pointer spans of size class 1 and above. These specialized mallocgc variants themselves
are faster than calling mallocgc, but the benefits of specializing decrease as the sizes
get larger: the allocation often gets dominated by needing to clear the memory, and at some point
the rest of the work of allocation becomes negligible. And it’s not enough to just be faster than
mallocgc! With size-specialized allocation, when the compiler knows which span class it needs to
allocate for, it can directly insert a call to the specialized function instead of the call to
newobject. But the compiler often doesn’t know which span class is being allocated when code
is generated: think slices of dynamic length.
Since the compiler can’t determine the size of the allocation, it will keep the call to mallocgc,
and mallocgc itself has to determine whether a specialized function is available, which one it is,
and then needs to call it. So the performance of the specialized function has to be high enough that even
with the overhead of a dynamic call it’s still faster.
This overhead issue isn’t the only problem. If it were, then we could create larger specialized
functions, and have them reserved for the compiler to insert them when the size is known at compile-time.
And if we didn’t call them dynamically we wouldn’t have to pay the dynamic overhead. But each specialized
function that’s added increases the sizes of the executables produced by the compiler, and, more importantly,
takes up precious instruction cache space. The single mallocgc function is often in the instruction
cache because of how frequently allocations happen. If we have too many specialized functions and
they’re not available in the cache, the overhead to retrieve the specialized code into the cache
can cancel out any benefits. And the more specialized allocation code that’s in the icache, the more
it crowds out the user code, making it slower to fetch and run user code. Doing a bunch of benchmarks
stopping at different size classes, we determined that stopping at 80 bytes was the sweet spot.
Of course, adding more specialized functions means more code to maintain. If each function were
hand-written, the code in the specialized functions could easily drift apart and go out of sync.
To help with this, we broke out the common parts of the specialized
functions and wrote an inliner using the standard library go/ast package to parse and format and
the golang.org/x/tools/go/ast/astutil package to manipulate the ASTs. The common parts of the functions
are all written in standard Go code that is built and typechecked with the rest of the runtime to
allow our tools to catch issues, but they are mostly just stubs for the inliner.
So we were able to measure improvements in the size-specialized allocation functions, but why are they actually
faster? The most apparent optimization is in clearing memory. The memory returned by mallocgc
does not always need to be zeroed, but it often does, and doing so can often take up most of the
time of the allocation. The memory clearing function
memclrNoHeapPointers is written in highly-optimized assembly, but we could do better
for the smaller clears. In a specialized function, if the size of the clear is constant, the
compiler can replace calls to memclrNoHeapPointers with code to directly produce the instructions
to clear the memory. The allocation can then skip a function call and some branches. This makes
a difference for the really small allocations, but as they get bigger, the function call overhead
becomes negligible.
While faster memory clearing provides the biggest improvement, there are some other tricks that are also possible in the specialized functions: Since they are specialized per span-class, the function doesn’t need to calculate the span class when retrieving the span. And because the size of the allocation is a constant, the compiler is able to do some optimizations to speed up the bookkeeping necessary for the allocation. One such case is with marking where the pointers are in the allocated memory. The specialized functions could also manually inline several of their helper functions. The Go compiler can inline code, but it avoids inlining functions that it considers too large. We can override that in the generated code by inserting the function bodies into the callers. With the generator we can produce copies of each of the bodies without needing to worry about each of the copies drifting. And we could move code that handled less common cases, such as the runtime debugging flags, into the slow path functions to make the specialized functions smaller.
While we hope this explanation of size-specialized allocation is interesting, you as a Go programmer don’t need to think about any of this when writing your code. Memory allocations will just be a little faster, with the biggest benefits going to some of the most common allocation sizes, especially the 16 and 24 byte allocations. These allocations are some of the most common because they consist of two or three 64-bit values, so they include allocations for things such as interface values and strings which have two values, or slices which have three. We spent a lot of time tuning the behavior of size specialized malloc and making sure the impact of the instruction cache effects will be minimal: we were originally planning to release size-specialized allocation in Go 1.26 but decided to wait an extra release to do extra tuning and cut down the additional code size as much as we could.
All you need to do to get the improved performance from size specialized allocations in your programs is to build them with Go 1.27. If you’re interested in more concrete actions you can take to improve memory allocation and garbage collection performance, please read the Go Garbage Collector Optimization Guide.
Although we are confident that size-specialized allocation should not cause regressions in your
code, if necessary, you can build your programs using GOEXPERIMENT=nosizespecializedmalloc to disable it.
If you do need to do this to solve an issue you’re experiencing with size-specialized allocation,
please file an issue at go.dev/issue/new so we can investigate it.
        
          
            Next article: Platform-independent SIMD in Go
Previous article: Goroutine Leak Profiles

title: Goroutine Leak Profiles
Google Summer of Code 2026 results
text:
The Rust Project participated in Google Summer of Code (GSoC) for the third time this year. This time we had 13 projects, and our dear contributors have been working very hard on them for several months. As usual, the projects had various durations, so while some of them have ended in August, the last one has only finished in November, so we have been waiting until we have all the results before publishing this blog post.
We are very happy to announce that all 13 projects were successful and passed their final evaluation! We consider it to be a testament to the diligence of our contributors, and the helpfulness of our mentors, that we are able to keep a very high rate[1] of successful GSoC projects several years in a row.
At the start of summer, we had a video call with our contributors, so that we could all get to know each other a bit, and learn about their projects. Over the following few months, we continuously communicated with the contributors, provided guidance and answered their questions and reviewed their pull requests. And most importantly, we learned many new things together! It was an overall great experience. We are grateful for all Rust contributions done by our GSoC participants and for the time we spent working together, and we hope that we will continue seeing at least some of them around in the future.
We would like to thank all our Rust GSoC 2026 contributors. You did a great job!
Even though this year we had fewer projects than in 2025, mostly due to limited mentoring capacity, Google Summer of Code 2026 was again a success for the Rust Project. We think that GSoC is a great way of introducing new contributors to our community, and we are looking forward to participating in GSoC (and other mentorship programs, such as Outreachy) again in the near future. If you are interested in becoming a (GSoC) contributor, check out our GSoC project idea list and our guide for new contributors.
Below you can find a brief summary of our GSoC 2026 projects. You can find more information about the original goals of the projects here. For easier navigation, here is an index of the project descriptions in alphabetical order:
And now strap in, as there is a ton of great content to read about here!
A Frontend for Safe GPU Offloading in Rust
- Contributor: Marcelo Domínguez
- Mentor: Manuel Drehwald
- Final report
Marcelo worked on improving the usability of cross-vendor GPU programs in Rust using the std::offload module. At the start of the project, the offload prototype was only a proof of concept. It assumed that the offloaded code was bug-free, and it required users to write a lot of boilerplate code. Marcelo resolved both issues over the summer.
First, he implemented proper type checking. Marcelo extended the compiler to verify that the arguments passed to any offload call are of the correct type, as expected by the GPU kernel. Kernel launches are thus now safe.
After that, he added support for generic kernels. The compiler now collects all generic instantiations launched from the CPU side, and loads that info later when compiling GPU kernels to make sure we instantiate them as needed. Marcelo also added support to select which GPU to use, which is helpful for laptops with both an integrated and a dedicated GPU, as well as for servers with multiple GPUs. He also added two macros that removed the need for any boilerplate when writing and launching GPU kernels.
The hardest part of this project by far was dealing with references. Due to Rust semantics, we cannot just map types containing mutable references to GPUs and then process them using multiple threads. Previous Rust GPU projects used raw pointers as a workaround, but we obviously wanted to avoid those. Marcelo managed to implement a sound abstraction so that users can now safely declare how their kernels will access mutable arguments.
As a cherry on top, Marcelo also ported the RajaPerf performance suite from C++ to Rust and used it to benchmark his pull requests. His safe Rust version matches the performance of the original C++ code, and is now described in a GPU offload paper that he is working on together with his mentor, Manuel. This was Marcelo's second Rust GSoC project, and same as last year, we are very happy with the results. Great job!
Adding WebAssembly Linking Support to Wild
- Contributor: Kei Akiyama
- Mentor: David Lattimore
- Final report
The goal of this project was simple on paper: teach the Wild linker to link WebAssembly (Wasm) programs. However, adding support for a new linker target is of course far from simple. Luckily, Kei already had a lot of experience with Wild, as this was his second GSoC project working on the Wild linker.
And as expected, Kei did a great job! Prior to GSoC 2026, Wild had no Wasm output support. Now, the Wasm support is sufficiently good that Wild can link a range of complex programs to Wasm. For example, it is able to link itself, SQLite, ripgrep, CPython and even the SpiderMonkey JavaScript engine.
And the linking performance is excellent! When compared to wasm-ld, the de-facto standard Wasm linker, which is based on the LLD linker, Wild is 2-15x faster, and uses 2-5x less memory. You can find more benchmarks in his final report, where he also explains that achieving this performance took quite some work, because Wild's ELF linking performance did not immediately translate to being fast when linking Wasm.
Even after this GSoC project ended, Kei has continued improving Wild's Wasm support, as well as contributing to other parts of Wild. Thank you for bringing fast linking to a new set of use-cases, Kei! You are a valued member of the Wild team.
Bringing autodiff and offload into Rust CI
- Contributor: Shota Sugano
- Mentor: Manuel Drehwald
- Final report
The goal of this project was to build the experimental std::autodiff module, which implements automatic differentiation of Rust code, and the std::offload module, which allows offloading Rust code to GPUs, in the CI of the Rust compiler.
Shota has already been contributing to this area in the months leading up to this year's GSoC, so he had no issues getting started. After valiantly fighting with our CI, he made both modules available in the official nightly compiler channel. Rust users can thus now simply install them with a single rustup command, rather than having to compile rustc from source! This is a huge benefit for gathering feedback on these features in the wild, as it makes it much easier to experiment with them.
Beyond making these projects available via rustup, he also worked on making it simpler to build projects that use std::offload. The original compilation pipeline was derived from Clang's support for GPU offload, so it involved calling clang helper binaries. That is clearly not optimal, so Shota worked on replacing it by directly calling the underlying LLVM APIs from rustc.
The last piece of his project was enabling testing in CI for both offload and autodiff, which already helped prevent multiple regressions. Right now, the GPU offload pipeline only tests the CPU setup side, but his work allowed us to talk to GPU hardware vendors, two of which already agreed to provide the Rust Project with GPU hardware so that in the future we can also run those tests on dedicated GPUs.
Overall, the project was a success. Shota had to show a lot of patience and endurance when working with various CMake quirks and CI challenges. We would like to extend a special thank you for that!
Debugger for Miri
- Contributor: Mohamed Ali
- Mentor: Oli Scherer
- Final report
miri is a tool that can detect undefined behavior (UB) in unsafe Rust code. It used to have a prototype of an interactive debugger called priroda, but it became unmaintained some time ago. The goal of this project was to re-establish priroda, to make it easier to use miri interactively, debug how and why is UB introduced in Rust programs, and also help rustc developers analyse MIR, one of the intermediate representations of Rust programs.
Mohamed successfully reached both main goals of this project. He created a miri interface for the gdb debugger, which allows debugging programs executed by miri. You can set breakpoints, step through individual instructions, analyse MIR local variables and inspect the debugged program's state, with miri acting as a "virtual CPU". So when you encounter your next miri UB report, you can actually debug the program state that caused UB by running priroda! Mohamed also created a command-line interface for priroda, which is used to test it in miri's CI. This will ensure that it keeps working properly and will not bitrot again.
Mohamed also added basic support for the Debugger Adapter Protocol, which allows using priroda together with IDEs such as Visual Studio Code. Currently, connecting priroda to an IDE is a bit involved, so the next step would be to build a plugin for an IDE that would allow showing all the extra state that miri has, which gdb doesn't know how to interpret.
Debugging programs executed by miri is very exciting. Thank you for all your work!
Implementing impl and mut restrictions
- Contributor: Ryosuke Yamano
- Mentors: Jacob Pratt, Urgau
- Final report
The goal of this project was to implement two new language features that were accepted in RFC 3323:
- Impl restrictions (impl(crate) trait Foo {}), which allow restricting in which modules you are able to implement a given trait.
- Mut restrictions (struct Foo { pub mut(crate) bar: u8 }), which allow restricting in which modules you are able to mutate a given field.
Ryosuke had to familiarize himself with the compiler's codebase and do a lot of implementation work to get both features working. This included implementing parsing of the new syntax, recording its metadata in the compiler's Abstract Syntax Tree, implementing resolution of the restricted crate paths, and finally adding checks to enforce both restriction rules. This all amounted to around five thousand lines of Rust code!
Once the new features were implemented and available on nightly, Ryosuke wrote a Call for Testing blog post. It had to be very exciting to announce to the world that he implemented two new features from scratch, and people can now play with them on the nightly channel! After the blog post was published, users reported a few issues, which Ryosuke promptly fixed. He also contributed to rustdoc to improve how the impl and mut restrictions are rendered in the generated documentation pages.
Now that the features are available on nightly, feedback is being gathered on them, with the plan being to stabilize them in 2027. If you would like to provide feedback on the impl and mut restrictions, you can do so in this issue.
The goal of this project was clear, and Ryosuke achieved it completely. Awesome work!
Improving Ergonomics and Safety of serialport-rs
- Contributor: Tanmay
- Mentor: Christian Meusel
- Final report
The goal of this project, which was done in collaboration with the Rust Embedded Working Group, was to improve the API ergonomics and type safety of the serialport-rs crate.
The serialport project is a bit different from some other projects which participated in this year's Google Summer of Code. It is more on the side of "facility management" than rocket science. Its challenges are taming finicky operating system APIs and making good abstractions, rather than full-blown software engineering.
Tanmay led many fruitful discussions about potential design decisions, and did a lot of field research on how other crates that depend on serialport actually use its API, to figure out how to make the upcoming breaking API changes less disruptive and painful for them.
Tanmay also worked on sanding off some rough edges of the serialport API, such as replacing Boxed trait objects with enums, and making errors explicit in places where the legacy API used to panic. Some of the work still waits for integration. It is targeting the upcoming serialport 5.0 release.
Christian (Tanmay's mentor) found working alongside Tanmay very motivational, and he was able to catch up with a lot of other unrelated work in order to integrate Tanmay's changes. He noted that working with Tanmay was fun and productive, and that it was pure joy to see him grow from his first contribution in the bonding phase to seasoned contributions. Thank you, Tanmay!
This was my first Google Summer of Code as well. It was challenging, motivating, fun and definitely worth it. I would show up again.
Christian Meusel
libc: transition differing bit-width time and offset variants and deprecate bug-prone constants
- Contributor: Adam Martinez
- Mentor: Trevor Gross
- Final report
libc is a foundational crate that is used by thousands of other crates across the Rust ecosystem. For the past several years, its maintainers have been attempting to publish a stable 1.0 release of the crate. Because this crate has to support interoperating with C on many compilation targets with weird quirks, this requires an enormous amount of work. We already had a GSoC project for moving libc towards 1.0 last year, and the goal of Adam's project was to make more progress in that direction.
And we can happily say that progress was indeed made! The original goal of Adam's project was to deprecate a number of constants that were difficult to maintain and cleanup inconsistencies in handling 32-bit/64-bit variants of file and time handling functions[2]. Adam was able to resolve that in a few weeks, and then he moved on to resolve a number of various issues blocking the 1.0 milestone.
Saying that Adam was productive would be… an understatement. We could follow his work in real-time, because he was posting daily GSoC reports for 116 days (!) in a row. The diligence and consistency with which he tackled so many complicated issues was an inspiration to us. In fact, sometimes the libc reviewers were not able to keep up!
You can find all Adam's libc pull requests here. You might notice that many of them have lots of comments, and even more discussions happened in GitHub issues and on Zulip. In addition to implementing the necessary code, making changes that affect interesting C platforms and architectures also required him to do a ton of research, and a lot of considerations of edge cases and possible backwards compatibility breakages. His work also took him on a whirlwind tour of diverse platforms; Adam's contributions spanned FreeBSD, NetBSD, Android, Hurd, NuttX, AIX, VxWorks, Fuchsia, L4Re and more.
Even though more work will still be required to get libc to 1.0, Adam's contributions made a significant dent in this effort. Thank you very much for all your work!
Link Linux kernel and its Modules with Wild
- Contributor: Vishruth Thimmaiah
- Mentor: David Lattimore
- Final report
Linker scripts are arcane commands that can be used to instruct a linker to construct the final binary in a custom way. The Wild linker used to implement only basic linker script functionality, which Vishruth greatly expanded during his GSoC project.
Thanks to that, Wild can now successfully link Linux kernel modules, and it's even close to being able to link the Linux kernel itself! Vishruth's work involved greatly expanding expression evaluation support, location counters, program headers, etc. In addition to adding support for many missing bits of linker script support, Vishruth implemented support for partial linking (-r) as this is needed in order to link Linux kernel modules. You can find all the linker script features that he implemented here.
Adding all those peculiar features to Wild required performing many cross-cutting changes to its codebase, which Vishruth managed to do really well. And it was not at the cost of performance! Wild now manages to link Linux kernel modules such as btrfs or amdgpu 2-4x faster than the BFD (GNU ld) or LLD linkers[3]. You can find more benchmarks in his final report.
Vishruth has continued to contribute to Wild even after his GSoC project ended and has become a valued contributor to the project. Thank you very much for making Wild better, Vishruth!
Migrating rust-analyzer assists to SyntaxEditor
- Contributor: bit-aloo
- Mentors: Chayim Refael Friedman, Lukas Wirth
- Final report
rust-analyzer uses rowan for its syntax trees, a library for Concrete Syntax Trees. rowan has served us well over the years, but it has some downsides that cause major performance problems and also smaller convenience issues. In particular, memory fragmentation causes rust-analyzer to consume much more memory than it actually needs (in the order of redundant gigabytes).
We wanted to rewrite rowan to change that. The problem was that many parts in rust-analyzer touch syntax trees, and in particular assists (code actions) of which we have a lot. They also use mutable tree editing, a feature of rowan that can be convenient but was a major obstacle in rewriting it to be more efficient.
During his project, bit-aloo first migrated all rust-analyzer code from mutable tree editing to SyntaxEditor, a new abstraction that was created specifically to avoid mutation. After that, he removed mutable editing from rowan altogether.
The migration process is incremental and rowan is still inefficient in various aspects. However, we believe that the parts which required changes to large amounts of code are behind us, and we can complete the migration with more focused changes. bit-aloo is continuing to work on that even after his GSoC project ended. And he was also accepted as a member of the rust-analyzer team, so congratulations! We would like to thank him for his work, and hope to continue working with him to improve rust-analyzer for everyone.
Port std::arch test suite to rust-lang/rust
- Contributor: Sumit Kumar
- Mentors: Jakub Beránek, Folkert de Vries
- Final report
The std::arch module of the Rust standard library contains various intrinsic functions that provide architecture and vendor-specific functionality. Their implementation lives in the stdarch repository, which is included as a Josh subtree in the main compiler repo (rust-lang/rust).
When someone changes the intrinsics in the main repo, breakages can silently creep in, because the main repo does not execute all the stdarch tests in its CI. That can cause friction when we synchronize the changes between the two repositories. Ideally, we would run all of stdarch's tests in the main repo to detect any issues as soon as possible.
And that is where Sumit came in! Over the course of his GSoC project, he examined the (very!) complex ways the intrinsics are tested in stdarch, and started porting them over to the main repo. But this was not a matter of copying over a few lines of YAML. The compiler repo uses its own build system (called bootstrap) and a CI workflow structure that is quite different from the stdarch repository. Sumit thus had to first understand what is each test suite doing, reimplement it as a part of bootstrap and finally integrate it into the compiler's CI workflows.
We run ~90 CI jobs across several hardware architectures, operating systems and OS versions. Getting all that to work while testing vendor-specific intrinsics required a lot of diligent work… and a lot of patience. It took five months for one of the test suites to finally succeed on the main repo's CI, and it required Sumit to completely refactor how the suite worked, for it to be more compatible with bootstrap. As another example, a different test suite that Sumit also got to work required running the tests in an Intel CPU emulator on CI.
Sumit ported most of the stdarch test suites to bootstrap, including intrinsics verification against reference C implementations, checks for automatically generated source code being up-to-date, and various unit tests for individual intrinsics and CPU feature detection logic. There is one remaining test suite to port, but the ported tests are already helping us find issues, which is great.
You can check Sumit's rust-lang PRs here; notice that he was also contributing to other parts of Rust in the meantime! Sumit's work will help us make LLVM upgrades and land intrinsics changes more easily. Thank you, Sumit!
Reorganizing tests/ui/issues
- Contributor: zedddie
- Mentors: Teapot, Kivooeo
- Final report
The goal of this project was to get rid of a very scary place in the Rust compiler's test suite: a directory called tests/ui/issues. It contained thousands of test files based on historical Rust issues, dating back all the way to 2012. The problem with those tests was that they were named only with an issue number (e.g. issue-37291). When such a test would break, it was quite difficult to figure out what was it even supposed to test, because there was little context attached to it.
Even though we already had a GSoC project to tackle this problem last year, due to the sheer amount of uncategorized tests, there were still over four hundred tests left in this directory by the time zedddie started working on this project.
For each test in this directory, zedddie had to first understand what was the test doing and dig through its original GitHub issue and any other related issues and pull requests. Then they had to figure out what would be the best location to move the test under, search for any possible duplicates, come up with a descriptive name for the test (that tends to be very difficult!), and finally add a short description to the test that explains the context of why the test was added in the first place. Rinse and repeat, for hundreds of tests.
zedddie rolled up their sleeves, and categorized over 300 tests in 30 pull requests. Together with other contributors helping out over this summer, zedddie was finally able to remove the last batch of uncategorized tests at the start of August. As zedddie said in their final report: "What is left to do: nothing, tests/ui/issues is gone".
While this work might sound a bit bland, its positive effect on the maintainability of our test suite, and improving the lives of Rust compiler contributors, is considerable. It is also apparently a great way to learn about cool niche edge cases of Rust that most Rust developers might not know about! After migrating the remaining uncategorized UI tests, zedddie continued contributing to the next trait solver and const generics. Thank you very much for helping us finally get rid of tests/ui/issues, zedddie!
Utilize debugger APIs to improve debug info test accuracy and error reporting
- Contributor: Anthony Bolden
- Mentors: Jakub Beránek, Jieyou Xu
- Final report
The Rust debugging experience leaves a lot to be desired. One reason why we struggled to improve it is that many of our debuginfo test suites did not even run in CI for the past few years, as they were difficult to maintain. When something changed in the type visualizers, the implementation details of a standard library type or in debugger internals, someone had to go through tens of tests and manually update them. This was not sustainable, so the test suite rotted.
Luckily for us, Anthony took that affront personally. Even before his GSoC project, he spent considerable effort on improving the quality of debug visualizers of various Rust standard library types, and gained an impressive amount of knowledge about debuggers.
During his GSoC project, he completely overhauled how our debuginfo test infrastructure works, both for LLDB and GDB. Thanks to his improvements, we can now easily "rebless" the reference output when something changes, which makes it much easier to keep our test suite up-to-date. The new tests also record much more information about the internal state of the debugger recorded during the test, which helps with diagnosing issues that cause type visualizers to stop working.
In addition to redesigning the test suite, Anthony also actually managed to re-enable the LLDB tests on both Windows and Linux in our CI again (after several years of being skipped there!). This will allow us to avoid debuginfo regressions and make it easier to improve the Rust debugging experience. Oh, and it goes without saying that while doing all that, he also made numerous improvements to Rust type visualizers. You can find his PRs here.
Anthony's amazing contributions and his deep expertise in debuggers led to him being invited to the Rust Compiler team, which was much deserved. What else can we add, other than: thank you for your awesome work!
XDG path support for rustup
- Contributor: Guicheng Liu
- Mentor: rami3l
- Final report
The support for platform-specific directories (platformdirs) has been a long-standing feature request for rustup, to have more fine-grained filesystem directory choices. This project investigated how that issue could be resolved.
The real complexity of this feature request lies within a decade worth of different assumptions that previous iterations of rustup and cargo have made: it turns out that quite a lot of them are no longer true if we were to implement platformdirs support truly faithfully.
Guicheng first worked on cleaning up the interactions between rustup self uninstall and $CARGO_HOME/bin as a warmup. This issue itself is a very good demonstration of all that compatibility baggage: somehow $CARGO_HOME/bin has become the default binary directory for all things Rust, so rustup ended up installing itself and all its proxies into it. As a result, it has been super annoying to many that everything in $CARGO_HOME is gone with rustup self uninstall.
After that, he started the actual implementation of platformdirs support in rustup. This was no easy task! Not because the code itself was hard to write, but because it takes a lot of effort to figure out what should be the desired behavior in the first place. Also, in order to determine the appropriate platformdirs semantics, some prior research is often required to see how things became what they are today, so the decoupling of different concerns could proceed, and migration paths could be designed accordingly. It was in this sense that this is different from a typical GSoC project, and luckily thanks to the effort he has put into this project, we have not only come up with the final patch, but also discovered and fixed some tiny preexisting issues with this long-untouched aspect of the rustup codebase along the way.
Thank you for digging into this complex topic, Guicheng!
Conclusion
