We would like to thank all contributors who have participated in Google Summer of Code 2026 with us! Your contributions helped make Rust better, and introduced you as new members of our community, which is a reason to celebrate. We are looking forward to participating in GSoC again next year!
We would also like to thank Google for organizing the Google Summer of Code program and for allowing us to host a large number of projects every year. And last, but not least, we would like to thank all the Rust mentors who were tirelessly helping our contributors to complete their projects. Without you, Rust GSoC would not be possible.
- 97.5% over a three-year period, if you are wondering (40 out of 41 projects were successful so far). ↩
- If you were wondering, then yes, this is actually related to the famous 2038 problem :) ↩
- In case you were wondering, the mold linker does not support linker scripts required to link Linux kernel modules at the moment, so Vishruth did not compare the performance of Wild against mold here. ↩

title: Announcing rustup 1.29.3
text:
The rustup team has published a new point release of rustup, 1.29.3.
Rustup is the recommended tool to install Rust, a programming language that empowers everyone to build reliable and efficient software.
What's new in rustup 1.29.3
This new patch release has fixed some minor regressions over the previous one:
- Fixed "Illegal instruction" error on certain x86_64 CPUs without SSE4.1. pr#5162
- Fixed "lock() not supported" error on Solaris. pr#5167
Further details are available in the changelog!
How to update
If you have a previous version of rustup installed, getting the new one is as easy as stopping any programs which may be using rustup (e.g. closing your IDE) and running:
$ rustup self update
Rustup will also automatically update itself at the end of a normal toolchain update:
$ rustup update
For this particular release, if you have encountered any issues during self-update, you may try to update rustup manually by following the steps below:
- Download the corresponding rustup-init binary for
your platform.
- Make double sure that no other rustup processes are running.
- Replace your existing rustup binary with the downloaded rustup-init renamed to rustup.
  - As a reminder, this binary is often located at $HOME/.cargo/bin/rustup, or $CARGO_HOME/bin/rustup if you have overridden the $CARGO_HOME environment
variable.
If you don't have it already, you can get rustup from the appropriate page on our website.
Rustup's documentation is also available in the rustup book.
Caveats
Rustup releases can come with problems not caused by rustup itself but just due to having a new release.
In particular, anti-malware scanners might block rustup or stop it from creating or copying
files, especially when installing rust-docs which contains many small files.
Issues like this should be automatically resolved in a few weeks when the anti-malware scanners are updated to be aware of the new rustup release.
Thanks
Thanks again to all the contributors who made this rustup release possible!

title: How to fund Rust contributors
text:
TLDR:
- To fund general maintenance, donate to the Rust Foundation Maintainers Fund or sponsor the RustNL Maintainers Team
- To fund specific features and improvements, sponsor fundable Rust Project Goals
- To fund individual contributors, donate to their GitHub Sponsors accounts
There is always so much to do in the Rust Project! New features to implement, bugs to fix, performance optimizations to make, issues to triage… It takes a lot of work to keep our high bar of quality while also shipping new features and improvements. And the workload keeps increasing with the continuous growth of Rust adoption.
As is unfortunately common in open source projects, a large fraction of that work is currently done by volunteers. That causes various issues, such as people burning out or complex features taking many years to ship.
Unsurprisingly, one of the best ways to help improve that is to get more people who work on Rust funded! This year, several funding initiatives started ramping up, and we already experience many positive effects. They helped us improve the maintenance status of critical Rust projects and make significant progress on several long-awaited features, such as allocators, the never type, the next trait solver or the Polonius borrow checker. However, only a fraction of people working on Rust are currently funded for their work.
We know that there are Rust users, both individuals and companies, who would like to help improve Rust by funding it, but it might not always be obvious how exactly to do that. This post thus provides suggestions on how you can support the development of Rust in three ways.
If you're unsure which option fits, or would like to discuss funding on behalf of your company, please contact the Funding team.
Fund general maintenance
Maintenance is a continuous process required to keep Rust (or any software project for that matter) working. It consists of two main activities. The first is general housekeeping, such as ensuring that Continuous Integration works, dependencies are kept up-to-date and issues, bugs and security incidents are promptly triaged and resolved. The second is performing refactorings and code reviews, which ensures that the codebase will be able to evolve and continuously ship new features, without accruing extensive technical debt.
Having quality maintenance is crucial for the long-term health of Rust, yet it is typically very difficult to find funding for it; funders often want to sponsor specific new features, rather than just "keeping the lights on". However, without sufficient maintenance, it becomes much more difficult, and much slower, to ship new features. Improving the maintenance of Rust thus also helps us ship features and improvements faster, though the effects are sometimes only observable over longer periods of time.
Funding maintenance is a great choice if you want to let us decide how best to improve Rust. The Rust Funding team continuously looks for Rust teams and projects that require help with their maintenance efforts, and allocates available funds to Rust maintainers who could help improve the situation.
To fund Rust maintainers, consider donating to the Rust Foundation Maintainers Fund or sponsoring the RustNL Maintainers Team.
Fund specific features and improvements
There are always many Rust improvements and new features that are in progress. We track some of those initiatives through Rust Project Goals. Each Goal describes a specific improvement to Rust: what it is, who is going to develop and drive it forward and which Rust teams are willing to help reviewing and maintaining it.
Some of those Goals are looking for funding. Either to help their owner dedicate time and focus to push the given feature forward, or to fund maintainers who will perform refactorings necessary to unblock that feature and review its implementation. Often funding is required for both. When a Goal is properly funded, the probability that it will achieve its milestones is much higher, which then translates in the given improvement being shipped sooner to Rust users.
Funding Project Goals is a great choice if you want to help push forward specific Rust features or Rust toolchain improvements that will benefit you or your company.
To fund contributors working on Project Goals, consider taking a look at Goals that need funding and reaching out to their funding contact. If in doubt how to proceed, reach out to the Rust Funding team.
Fund individual contributors
There are hundreds of people in the Rust Project who continuously work on improving Rust. Some of them have personal fundraising profiles (e.g. on GitHub Sponsors), which allows you to support them directly.
There might be various reasons for supporting a specific person. Maybe they are maintaining a crate that you love to use, maybe you like reading their blog posts, or maybe you are simply a fan of the work that they do. Whatever the reason, we are sure that they would appreciate your support!
Funding individual contributors is a great choice if you want to directly support Rust contributors whose work you appreciate.
To fund individual Rust contributors, check out their GitHub profile or personal website to see what options there are for supporting them. You can also examine our list of Rust Project members who can be supported through GitHub Sponsors[1].
Conclusion
We hope that this post is useful to anyone who would potentially like to invest funds into making Rust better. You can also find a shortened version of the "how to fund Rust guide" at the Funding page of the Rust website, or check out a RustConf 2026 talk by Niko Matsakis about how Project Goals and their funding works.
If you are a company looking to fund the development of Rust, consider joining the Rust Commercial Network. Joining the network is free, and Rust Foundation membership is not required. It can help you find opportunities for funding improvements in specific areas related to Rust usage (e.g. user interfaces, language interop, supply chain security, etc.) and collaborate on funding Rust development with other companies.
There are of course other ways of helping Rust other than donating funds. For example, you can check out Project Goals that are looking for contributors or more generally check our contributor onboarding guide. Companies can also help by giving employees paid time to contribute upstream, or by hiring Rust contributors to do that work. One possible model is the Engineer in Residence role, that was recently established in the Rust Foundation.
- Note that this list is not exhaustive; there are some Project members who accept donations through GitHub Sponsors (or another fundraising platform), but did not opt into being listed on this page. ↩

title: Announcing rustup 1.29.2
text:
The rustup team is happy to announce the release of rustup version 1.29.2.
Rustup is the recommended tool to install Rust, a programming language that empowers everyone to build reliable and efficient software.
What's new in rustup 1.29.2
This is a small release which only updates the rustls-webpki and webpki-root-certs dependencies to address the problematic eMudhra intermediate certificates issue described in CVE-2026-111943.
See also RUSTSEC-2026-0382.
Further details are available in the changelog!
How to update
If you have a previous version of rustup installed, getting the new one is as easy as stopping any programs which may be using rustup (e.g. closing your IDE) and running:
$ rustup self update
Rustup will also automatically update itself at the end of a normal toolchain update:
$ rustup update
If you don't have it already, you can get rustup from the appropriate page on our website.
Rustup's documentation is also available in the rustup book.
Caveats
Rustup releases can come with problems not caused by rustup itself but just due to having a new release.
In particular, anti-malware scanners might block rustup or stop it from creating or copying
files, especially when installing rust-docs which contains many small files.
Issues like this should be automatically resolved in a few weeks when the anti-malware scanners are updated to be aware of the new rustup release.
Thanks
Thanks again to all the contributors who made this rustup release possible!

title: Announcing Rust 1.99.1
text:
The Rust team has published a new point release of Rust, 1.99.1. Rust is a programming language that is empowering everyone to build reliable and efficient software.
If you have a previous version of Rust installed via rustup, getting Rust 1.99.1 is as easy as:
rustup update stable
If you don't have it already, you can get rustup from the appropriate page on our website.
What's in 1.99.1
Rust 1.99.1 fixes the following regressions from prior releases:
- Missing symbol wcslen: Some Rust targets were getting link errors for missing wcslen, and that function is now present in Rust's compiler-builtins library as a fallback.
The LLVM loop-idiom-wcslen pass may introduce calls to wcslen as an optimization, and some Rust targets did not have that function readily available in libc or elsewhere. The UEFI targets in particular were broken for any project using std, as some of these calls were introduced in the precompiled standard library, but the issue was also reproducible for similar user code patterns.
- Miscompilation of FFI bool return values on x86_64: Rust functions returning bool through FFI could leave bits 1-7 of the return register unspecified, causing callers to observe raw values other than 0 or 1. This return type is now marked for zero-extension again, as required by the ABI.
- rust-lld failed to load libLLVM on macOS: This linker could fail to run if the compiler was invoked without the rustup proxy, as there was no direct setting for the appropriate library search path. Now rust-lld is built with an rpath entry for the directory containing libLLVM.dylib.
If you'd like to help us out by testing future releases, you might consider using the beta (rustup default beta) and nightly (rustup default nightly) channels locally and in your CI. Please report any bugs you might come across!
Contributors to 1.99.1
Many people came together to create Rust 1.99.1. We couldn't have done it without all of you. Thanks!

title: Demoting i686 Windows targets to std-only
text:
With Rust 1.100.0, the following changes to 32-bit Windows targets will happen:
- i686-pc-windows-msvc Tier 1 with host tools target will be demoted to Tier 1 without host tools.
- i686-pc-windows-gnu Tier 2 with host tools target will be demoted to Tier 2 without host tools.
Builds of the standard library will continue to be distributed, but host tools such as the compiler will be no longer available. i686-pc-windows-msvc as a Tier 1 target still undergoes CI testing.
To build 32-bit Windows binaries, cross-compiling from a still-supported host toolchain (such as a 64-bit Windows ones) will be required from now on.
Background
Desktop and Server 32-bit only x86 CPUs are no longer sold for over 15 years, and general 32-bit Windows support has ended in October 2025. This means that the development platforms these targets are meant for hardly exist these days, and even if they do exist they typically aren't capable enough for development.
Even on the modern x86_64 hardware, building i686 Windows toolchains has proven to be problematic. We have encountered compiler binaries crashing when built with the i686 MSVC target, and the GNU C++ toolchain failing with OOMs during LLVM build.
Considering all these things, cross-compiling these targets from a better supported one is what we have found to be the best solution forward. As part of that, we stopped producing host tools for these targets. For the time being, the prebuilt standard library is still available, and in case of i686-pc-windows-msvc still tested on CI.
What Changes?
After Rust 1.100, it will no longer be possible to install toolchains on 32-bit Windows hosts. We recommend cross-compiling from a still-supported host (such as a 64-bit Windows toolchain) instead. Other 32-bit platforms are not impacted by this change.
For more details about these demotions, see RFC 3999 for i686-pc-windows-msvc demotion, and MCP 1020 for i686-pc-windows-gnu demotion.

title: Announcing Rust 1.99.0
text:
The Rust team is happy to announce a new version of Rust, 1.99.0. Rust is a programming language empowering everyone to build reliable and efficient software.
If you have a previous version of Rust installed via rustup, you can get 1.99.0 with:
$ rustup update stable
If you don't have it already, you can get rustup from the appropriate page on our website, and check out the detailed release notes for 1.99.0.
If you'd like to help us out by testing future releases, you might consider updating locally to use the beta channel (rustup default beta) or the nightly channel (rustup default nightly). Please report any bugs you might come across!
What's in 1.99.0 stable
extern "C" variadics
Rust 1.99.0 stabilizes defining C-ABI variadic functions with "C" and
"C-unwind" ABIs. Variadic functions defined this way use a variable argument
list (...) and accept an arbitrary number of arguments. Rust could already
call externally-defined variadic functions (e.g., libc::printf). With Rust
1.99, these functions can now be written in Rust itself:
/// SAFETY: must be called with (at least) 2 i32 arguments.
unsafe extern "C" fn sum(mut args: ...) -> i32 {
    // SAFETY: guaranteed by the caller.
    let a = unsafe { args.next_arg::<i32>() };
    let b = unsafe { args.next_arg::<i32>() };
    a + b
}
fn foo() -> i32 {
    unsafe { sum(0i32, 2i32) }
}
The type of ... is VaList,
which is ABI-compatible with the C va_list type across targets. What types can be read from a VaList is guarded by the
VaArgSafe trait.
For more details on c-variadic functions, see the Reference. This release also stabilizes support for defining naked variadic functions with non-"C" ABIs, which must be written via inline assembly.
Layout information from raw pointers
This release settles the safety requirements for retrieving the size and
alignment on raw pointers to both Sized (trivially safe, already possible on
stable) and non-Sized types.
This is done by stabilizing three functions:
Recommend against round-trip unleaking after Box::leak
While there are no changes to the language semantics in Rust 1.99, we have
updated the documentation on Box::leak to recommend against patterns that
later deallocate that memory. This was done because such code was found to have
problematic interactions with current and future potential compiler optimizations,
and is especially problematic with the upcoming stabilization of custom allocators.
Instead, Box::into_non_null or Box::into_raw should be preferred.
This guidance also applies to other leak functions in the standard library.
Stabilized APIs
Other changes
Check out everything that changed in Rust, Cargo, and Clippy.
Contributors to 1.99.0
Many people came together to create Rust 1.99.0. We couldn't have done it without all of you. Thanks!

title: Announcing a Maintainer in Residence: Scott Schafer for the Cargo team
text:
At the end of August, we announced our first Maintainers in Residence, Rust Project contributors who are funded for their upstream contributions and maintenance work from the Rust Foundation Maintainers Fund (RFMF). Since then, the Rust Leadership Council has dedicated more funds from its Project Priorities budget to RFMF, and together with AWS also providing additional funds, this allowed us to open a new full-time Maintainer in Residence (MiR) position to support the Cargo team. We would like to thank the Rust Leadership Council, AWS, and also the Rust Foundation for providing us with this opportunity! If you would like to help us hire more maintainers to improve Rust, consider donating to RFMF.
This post explains why we chose to support the Cargo team specifically, and introduces Scott Schafer, the new Cargo Maintainer in Residence.
Why Cargo?
The new MiR full-time position is dedicated to helping with the maintenance of Cargo, our build system and package manager. The Cargo project is deeply involved in many new Rust features, improvements, and Project Goals. Combined with its cross-cutting nature, where it has to support many different use-cases and integrate with several other tools, it takes a lot of work just to keep up with its maintenance needs, let alone support so many feature requests and proposed changes.
Because of that, the Cargo team has sometimes struggled with meeting its maintenance demands. You might remember that for several years, it actually held a feature freeze, to reduce Cargo's internal tech debt, perform necessary refactorings, go through the issue and pull request backlog, and come up with scalable internal development and design processes, so that they could eventually go back to even thinking about adding new features.
Recently, some changes occurred within the team, which made it more difficult for them to meet their maintenance baseline. Some members of the team left, while others lost their dedicated funding for working on Cargo maintenance and had to scale down their involvement. The Funding team thus considered it very important to support this team, given that we had an opportunity to do so. And thus we decided to hire a full-time maintainer to work on Cargo for (at least) the next 12 months.
Even though we know that a single full-time maintainer will not completely solve the maintenance struggles of the Cargo team, we hope that it will improve the situation, and provide a bit of a relief for the team.
Introducing Scott Schafer
We are very happy to welcome Scott Schafer (@muscraft) into the Maintainer in Residence role! Scott has joined the Cargo team three years ago, and apart from working on Cargo, he is also the lead of the Rust Docker team, which prepares official Docker images for every Rust version.
Apart from working on general maintenance of Cargo, Scott has implemented Cargo's Workspace inheritance feature, and has also spearheaded a complex multi-year effort to switch the rendering of diagnostics in the Rust compiler to use the annotate-snippets crate. This effort has been completed in the Rust 1.93.0 release. Thanks to it, the same diagnostics interface can now be shared between the compiler and Cargo (and also other tools), which amongst other things unblocked further development of the Cargo linting system, which has now been stabilized and will ship in the Rust 1.100.0 release.
Everyone we talked about was very excited about Scott becoming a Cargo Maintainer in Residence, and we share that feeling. We wish Scott all the best in his new role, and we are very happy that we can support his maintenance work.
Here is what Scott thinks about it:
I am incredibly excited to work on Cargo full-time! There have been so many things that I wish I could've worked on over the years, that I will now be able to get to. I hope that my efforts will bring Cargo into a more maintainable state.
Conclusion
We are incredibly happy that we keep getting more funds for the Rust Foundation Maintainers Fund, which allows us to support Rust Project contributors. The funding team will be working with the supported maintainers, and also the funders, to ensure that they are all happy with the arrangement, so that we can secure stable funding for Rust maintenance for years to come.
If you would like to help us support more Rust maintainers, consider donating to RFMF!

title: GitHub Actions leaking secrets when Miri output is cached
text:
The Rust Security Response Team was notified that Miri stores all environment variables to target/, allowing secrets to persist in caches.
While not necessary a vulnerability in and of itself, when paired with GitHub Actions caching behavior, it is possible for this to expose secrets to PRs.
Overview
GitHub Actions makes it possible to cache directories between runs. Typical setups allow CI runs on main (and other branches) to write to cache, and PRs can only read from cache (preventing cache poisoning). Rust projects tend to speed up CI by caching binaries built by cargo install and sometimes the contents of target/.
PR CI can be triggered by anyone who can open PRs on your repository. GitHub requires maintainer approval for the first PR, but future PRs will rerun CI on every push. Anyone who has previously landed a change can trigger a CI run extracting information from cached target/ and then cover their tracks by pushing a second commit to the PR.
GitHub sometimes hides overwritten commits in its UI, making this kind of attack harder to detect. CI run logs and overwritten commits are also deleted after a few months.
When cargo miri is invoked, Miri needs to retain build-relevant environment variables between runs[1]. The current code to do so achieves this by storing all environment variables to target/. This, of course, persists when target/ is cached.
If your environment contained secrets, these can now be accessed by PRs via the cache.
Our fix
Our short term fix for this is to make Miri only preserve CARGO_* environment variables (excepting CARGO_*_TOKEN) and OUT_DIR. In the longer term, Miri and cargo may figure out better ways to inform Miri of the relevant list of environment variables. Note that this patch may not be available on nightly yet.
We also performed an ecosystem scan of GitHub repositories and identified 1 repository with this issue and 7 repositories that do not appear to be vulnerable but should be cautious anyway. We have reached out to those maintainers.
Am I affected?
It is likely that our scan was imperfect, so we recommend you check your own GitHub Actions setups if you run Miri.
You are vulnerable if:
- You run cargo miri in CI
- The step that runs cargo miri has access to secrets as an environment variable:
  - By being passed in to the step itself as an environment variable
  - By being set in env for the workflow
  - By being passed in to a previous step that persists it in the environment somehow
- The workflow being used caches the target directory, usually done via actions/cache or swatinem/rust-cache
- The cache is accessible to PRs (common and often the intended use case)
Possible quick fixes include:
- Disabling cache for that job.
- Scoping secrets to steps in that job that do not call Miri.
- Temporarily disabling Miri.
Once done, please clear the cache. Consider rotating any secrets that might have leaked.
The Miri release in the upcoming nightly (2026-09-22) will no longer have this problem.
Even if you do not run Miri, ensure jobs that can write to public caches do not have access to secrets. Many tools do not have special handling for secrets, and assume the entire environment can be written to the filesystem.
Threat model
We consider it bad practice to have a cache that can easily be tainted by secrets.
If caching target/, it is worth making sure that the inputs to processes that create target/ (anything invoking cargo) do not have secrets available. It is generally rare for standard cargo build/test subcommands to need any secrets or tokens[2], so this is mostly a matter of being careful about having secrets exposed as environment variables to the entire job.
Cargo/Miri/Rust does not guarantee that environment variables will be safe from being copied into target/. While we are treating this as a security issue and patching it out of an abundance of caution, this is not something you should rely on in general. Beyond official Rust tooling, it is possible for build scripts to be doing things that lead to the environment being stored in compilation artifacts.
Acknowledgements
Thanks to Predrag Gruevski of OpenAI for reporting this issue to us. Furthermore, the ecosystem scan was performed using Codex access and credits donated by OpenAI, which we also thank them for.
Issue triage and remediation was performed by Manish Goregaokar, Ralf Jung, Ben Kimock, Weihang Lo, Jacob Finkelman, Walter Pearce, Josh Stone, and Mark Rousskov.

title: Be alert: targeted attacks on prominent Rustaceans
text:
We believe that there is an ongoing campaign targeting rust-lang members and owners of popular crates that is attempting to compromise devices and accounts in order to use them to publish malware.
What we've seen
A video call is set up for something positive — maybe for a job, maybe for a project, maybe for a contract opportunity — and then that's used as a vector to either get the target to install something on their computer (such as a purportedly missing audio codec) or execute another command (for example, via putting a command on the clipboard).
These attackers are setting up new but legitimate seeming company profiles, including plausible LinkedIn presences, in order to pass cursory inspection.
A previous attack of this form targeted many prominent Rust developers in
June, and, last month, the arrayref crate was briefly compromised through similar
attacks. At this moment we do not know if these are all a part of the same
campaign.
This attack style is known to be used by the DPRK, and has been seen outside of the Rust community as well.
What you can do
Please take extra care in the near term. Be appropriately suspicious of cold outreaches, and ensure that any calls you have with new people are on platforms you trust — ideally, try to be the one who sets up the call on a platform you already use.
Please also re-check that your accounts look normal: MFA enabled, no unexpected logins on platforms that can track that, and so on.
If you have any concerns about your accounts, please reach out to help@crates.io (for crates.io account concerns) and/or security@rust-lang.org (for any other concerns). We're very happy to help.

title: Maintainer spotlight: Anthony Bolden (@Walnut356)
text:
There are hundreds of people who maintain the Rust toolchain, often on a volunteer basis on top of another job. The Rust Content team is working on a series of blog posts highlighting some of these prolific contributors to recognize the awesome work that they are doing in order to make Rust better for everyone. You can find the previous post here. Consider donating to the Rust Foundation Maintainers Fund if you'd like to support Rust Project maintainers.
In this post, we would like to introduce Anthony Bolden (@Walnut356). Anthony is a self-taught programmer who went on a mission to improve the Rust debugger experience. This year, he participated as a contributor in the Google Summer of Code program, and recently he joined the Rust compiler team.
We interviewed Anthony to find out what brought him to programming and how he became an expert on debuggers. Read more below!
Can you briefly introduce yourself and tell us how you started with programming?
Hello, my name is Anthony Bolden, also known as @Walnut356, and I live in Wisconsin. I do not have any formal computer science education and I've never had a job in the tech industry, so my journey to programming was a bit different. I work overnight shifts in a hotel, where I often have a lot of time to spare, and I needed something to occupy my mind. For I while, I used to solve puzzles or read books, but eventually I got tired of that.
I wanted to find a long-term project, so I tried programming. It took me a couple of tries until it "clicked", but when that happened, I instantly fell in love with it. It is so much fun!
How did you discover Rust?
I bought a couple of C++ books when I was learning how to program, so that was my entrypoint. But I was very dissatisfied with the development experience there. I wanted to make a simple game, because I've always found game design fascinating, but adding a dependency like SDL to my project turned out to be very difficult. I spent SO MUCH time trying to get it to work, and it didn't help that I was doing it on Windows. It should not be that hard!
I really enjoy low-level programming, optimization work, reading assembly for fun… but C++ was not for me. So I switched to Python, even though I was not super satisfied with its performance and its typical use-cases. At the time, I played Super Smash Bros. Melee competitively, and I wanted to analyze replays from my matches to improve my play. There was an existing Python replay parser, but it was outdated and slow. I forked it, and through painstaking effort I managed to double its performance. But when working with thousands of replays and gigabytes of data, it still took an hour to process everything in Python.
Then I realized that the original author of the Python parser abandoned it because they ran into the same performance problems. They decided to rewrite it in Rust instead. I took a look at the Rust code, but it seemed really complicated. It took me a few tries to break through the syntax barrier, but it didn't take long to realize that Rust is exactly where I wanted to be. It gave me the power to express exactly what I wanted, it was incredibly fast, and I didn't have to constantly fight just to add a dependency or build my project.
You are doing a lot of work in the area of debuggers. What started that interest?
When I started with Rust, I solved a lot of Advent of Code tasks, and I was debugging constantly, because it was my first exposure to data structures and algorithms.
One day, CodeLLDB, which is a Visual Studio Code debugger plugin that I was using, removed their built-in Rust support, instead falling back to the visualizer scripts Rust distributes in its toolchains. That instantly made my debugging experience terrible, because those scripts weren't part of MSVC toolchains, and there were no alternatives at the time that would enable debugging with LLDB on Windows.
Luckily, we programmers have a superpower: we can fix our own tools. At first, I wanted to contribute to either CodeLLDB, LLDB or LLVM itself to improve things. I've always been very interested in developer tooling anyway, so this was the perfect excuse to get started. However, trying to work with the LLVM codebase on Windows was just abysmal. I could not get my editor's C++ language plugin to work on its codebase, so I might have as well have been writing code in Notepad. After several weeks of frustration, I started looking into other options.
The CodeLLDB maintainer suggested that it might be possible to fix the debugger visualizers on the Rust side. I was very pleased with the Rust tooling experience so far, but I was worried that building the Rust compiler would be an absolute nightmare, just like with LLVM. I cloned the Rust repo, ran the build command, and it just worked. On the first try, without any errors. I immediately thought "I need to put all of my focus on this". It was absolutely beautiful, there was no "environment hell" to work through before I could start writing code.
Dealing with debugger internals sounds complicated. How did you learn it?
I read through the CodeLLDB debuginfo visualizers, and it spiraled from there. When I find something I don't understand, I immediately open a new browser tab and look into it. That often leads to something else I don't understand, until I suddenly realize that I have 70 browser tabs open. There is an unbelievable amount of complexity in all this.
How did you start contributing to Rust?
Back in 2024, the Rust toolchain did not distribute debuginfo visualizers on Windows. Fixing that was one of my first contributions. Then I got started fixing all the little details that prevented the scripts from working properly for programs compiled for MSVC. Back then, the Rust compiler debuginfo test suite did not work on Windows at all, so I had to provide "proof" that my pull requests worked via screenshots. It was pretty silly, and not very reliable.
Sometimes, I work on debuginfo improvements out of spite, because I'm a bit mad about the state of debugging in Rust when working on my own projects. But in general, I want to improve it also for everyone else, because many people are dissatisfied with it. It feels nice and rewarding to be able to take something (like the LLDB debugging experience on Windows) from not working at all to working reasonably well.
Due to my background, I don't have a college thesis or some sort of big project that I could be proud of, so having something that I can collaborate on with a large amount of people and be able to genuinely help out feels super good. The Rust Project is actually one of the nicest communities that I ever interacted with, everybody has been super kind and helpful.
This year, you participated in Google Summer of Code. How did you find it?
I heard about Google Summer of Code in 2025, but at the time, I didn't feel confident enough in my skills to participate. Looking back, I maybe could have done it, but I didn't have a project in mind anyway. Eventually, I realized that I would probably never feel confident enough in my coding skills. I had to just try it. This year, after discussing the testing situation with the compiler team, I applied for a project to improve the state of Rust compiler debuginfo tests.
When I was in high school, I had some difficulty with long-term, self-structured projects, so I was a bit worried about how it would go. But in the end, I think it went better than I would have expected. I stayed motivated, consistently worked on my project, and I think that I made really good progress on the goals that we set out.
I think I improved in a lot of programming-adjacent skills too. It used to be very difficult for me to keep up with having multiple pull requests open at once, constantly switching between different git branches while staying organized. I feel like I got much better at that.
I also became more confident in the whole contribution process. Opening a single pull request actually used to be a very big deal to me! I talked to my girlfriend about it, kept her updated whenever I got a review or it got merged, it was a whole thing. Nowadays, I open 2 or 3 pull requests at once, and it's not a big deal anymore.
After finishing your GSoC project, you were invited to the Rust Compiler team. What does that mean to you?
I got blindsighted by it! I was going to ask about the process for joining the compiler team that I would have to go through, but before I even asked, I was invited to the team. I'm still kind of in shock, to be honest. When I accepted it, I looked at the list of compiler team members, whose blog posts I have been reading for years. I don't have the sort of background, or a PhD, or a prestigious job at a giant tech company that many of them have. I look up to them and respect them so much, and it is such an honor to be working alongside them and learning from them.
It will sound silly, but when I appeared on the Rust website after becoming a member of the team, it brought me to tears. I worked really hard the past couple of years, and it's easy to think "my code isn't good enough" or "what I'm doing isn't important". It is very cool that I was able to follow through with something that I set out to do, and I was recognized by other people for it. Since being added to the compiler team, I actually found out that my background is not that unique, and that there are others in the compiler team that are self-taught! It's really reassuring.
Participating in GSoC and joining the compiler team also made it easier to explain to others what it is that I do. Trying to explain how open source works to my grandparents was difficult, because it almost sounds like a scam. It helps a lot when I can show them on the Rust website that I am now a part of the team that maintains the compiler. It is something tangible that they can brag to their friends about.
What are you working on right now?
Now that the debuginfo testing situation is no longer so dire, it freed me up to start adding new features to the debugger visualizers. I want to improve the visualizers for the Vec type and for wide pointers, allow indexing hashmaps in the debugger, and much more. There is also a large number of performance wins that we could achieve.
Recently, I learned that LLDB maintainers plan to improve their plugin interface, which might allow us to have a native Rust debugging integration. That would allow implementing much better expression parsing and maybe integrating the debugger with miri. Another idea is that we could ship debuginfo visualizers written in Rust.
Would you like to work on Rust professionally?
If I could work on improving Rust debuginfo full-time, that would actually be the dream for me. I have a lot of fun with this, and I did it both during my night shifts, and in my free time. I would love to have a programming job in general, though I guess I sort of chose the wrong time to get into the industry, with the state of the job market right now. The hotel I worked for reduced the number of night auditors recently, and my position was eliminated. It's a bit bittersweet, since the stability and downtime are what allowed me to start programming in the first place, but I take it as a sign that it's time to move forward with my career and start seriously applying for software engineering positions.
What advice would you give someone just starting their Rust journey?
When you are starting to learn Rust, don't worry about best practices too much. Experiment, push boundaries, try everything, even if your code looks a bit gross. If the compiler tells you no, and you think it should work anyway, then argue with it! Try different things, do your research, and find out why it works the way that it does. If you just blindly follow best practices from the start, you might end up with a tunnel vision and not learn some important lessons.
We thank Anthony for sharing his thoughts with us, and for all his work on improving the Rust debugging experience! You can read more about his debuginfo adventures on his blog.

title: Variadic Generics Micro Survey results
text:
A year ago, we launched the Variadic Generics Micro Survey, with the goal of collecting people's use cases for a hypothetical variadic generics feature.
Because of its open-ended purview, this survey included a lot of open answers. Not only that, respondents were encouraged to fill out answers, in as much detail as they wanted. And they did: we got over 3300 submissions, including 900 text answers to just one question.
We fed these answers to Claude and it told us th- ha, just kidding, if only.
More seriously, we did consider using AI to process the answers, but decided not to over privacy and quality concerns. Instead we ended up going through the dataset by hand, hence why these results took so long to publish.
This article will include both the numerical survey results and some trends observed in the free answers. See also the full report, which includes the polls and examples of answers showcasing the trends.
Table of contents
Background
This first questions were about users' backgrounds.
How long have you been using Rust?
Have you heard about variadic generics before?
Where have you heard about variadic generics?
Among the open responses, the most common were:
The "solving a problem" category is interesting: a few people mentioned wanting to solve a specific problem, doing some research, and finding that they wanted was called "variadic generics".
Here we can already notice the Bevy community is somewhat over-represented in the answers. It's not clear to what extent this is because Bevy users care a lot about variadics, or because there was a lot of advertising for the survey on the Bevy Discord server.
First use-cases
This code example was given to illustrate variadic generics (with pseudocode syntax):
impl<...Ts: SomeTrait> SomeTrait for (...Ts) {
    fn do_stuff(&self) -> u32 {
        let mut sum = 0;
        for member in ...self {
            // The trait bounds ensure each member has a do_stuff() method
            sum += member.do_stuff();
        }
        sum
    }
}
let value: u32 = (0, 0.5, "hello", Some("hello"), false).do_stuff();
Users then saw this question:
Are there cases where variadic generics would have made your project easier?
This was the question with the most open answers: of the 1702 people who said yes above, 1025 gave more detail, from single-line answers to multi-page explanations.
We've split the open answers into rough categories:
Some quotes (copied verbatim):
Almost any time you implement a trait for a tuple you almost always want to implement it for all tuple sizes. I've usually seen this done with macros up to some fixed size.
I have a parser combinator library. As a parser combinator sugar i had to overload varying number of tuples with their own trait impls. That was annoying
Mainly around querying (sql) with variable number of columns and / or parameters. This is worked around with macros (a la sqlx) but could be more elegant with tuples.
I would love to have them for more explicit multi dimensional tensor types. Like Tensor<5,7,9>, this would easily catch dimensions mismatch on building neural networks, for instance.
Struct-of-Arrays vector wants to decompose a type (struct or enum) into its fields: a tuple of field types or a tuple of field pointers is thus needed. Variadics could be helpful here
(See this document for a list of quotes illustrating each of those categories.)
Some people mentioned wanting variadics for a specific project:
A lot of people mentioned wanting to replace macros, or using macros as a substitute for variadics. Most people were neutral about this. A few (about 7) explicitly declared the macros workaround were enough for them.
More people mentioned strongly disliking the macro workaround, for various reasons:
A few answers mentioned implementing the macro workaround for tuples up to a given size, and then finding out that size wasn't enough for their users.
I've made safe Rust bindings for C libraries with variadic functions that use printf(3)-style formatting. In doing so, I had to do a fair bit of work to support multiple numbers of arguments... and inevitably a use-case came up which required more arguments (and thus longer tuples) than had been provided for.
The most interesting answers are people who explicitly mentioned they gave up on a feature or an approach because of the lack of variadics.
These days it's more about the opportunity loss: I know this is impossible, so I don't even think about reaching out for tuples of items implementing the same trait. I'm sure I've written situations where I had to use Vec<Box<dyn Trait>> not because I wanted boxed elements, but because the more natural thing (tuples of differently-typed values all implementing a single trait of arbitrary length) doesn't exist.
Sometimes I have also wanted to implement some crate-local trait for tuples but have found it too cumbersome due to the necessity to use a macro to do it, so I never bothered, even though I sort of wanted to.
The current "solution"--as I'm sure you're aware--is the classic macro that implements some trait for a tuple of length N of generic parameters. That is so uncomfortable, slow, complex and error-prone I have seen many examples (as a contributor of bevy) where variadric generics were the best solutions to a given problem, but they were rejected because they were not worth the trouble for the current problem (compilation time, mainly).
Variadic mappings
This code example was given to illustrate variadic mappings:
impl<...Ts> UnwrapAll for (Option<...Ts>) {
    type Unwrapped = (...Ts);
    fn unwrap_all(self) -> Self::Unwrapped {
        for option in ...self {
            option.unwrap()
        }
    }
}
let my_gift_boxes = (Some(1), Some(true), Some("hello"));
let opened_gifts = my_gift_boxes.unwrap_all();
assert_eq!(opened_gifts, (1, true, "hello"));
Users then saw this question:
Are there cases where variadic mappings would have made your project easier?
Of the 1287 people who said yes, 344 included free answers.
Overall, most of the free answers were variants of "Yes, it would be nice" or "Same use-case as the previous question":
This feature would also be helpful for the use case described previously.
I should add that, in general, probably 90% of the time I make a macro, it's for something that could be a variadic mapping.
this would actually be helpful in every-day code
I've had several instances of traits that make sense for tuples, but also have an associated type that should be "tupled" as well.
A few people pointed out that the pseudo-code syntax in the example was confusing:
the syntax of <Option ...Ts> is kinda awkward for the first sight. It feels like it would be better to see something like ...Option<Ts>. It's a tuple of a few options, not the Option of some tuple. Thanks for the survey!
Because the free answers are overall similar to the ones we already discussed, we'll skip straight to the next section.
Non-linear variadics
This code example was given to illustrate non-linear generics:
fn get_children<...Ts>(parents: (...Ts)) -> (for <T of ...Ts where T: Parent> T::Child) {
    for parent in ...parents where parent: Parent {
        parent.child()
    }
}
Users then saw this question:
Are there cases where non-linear mappings would have made your project easier?
In retrospect, the example is clearly too leading. The question was supposed to point to any kind of operation on lists of types beside "one-to-one mapping"; but the example oriented responses towards filtering specifically. That example would also, if allowed, be a workaround for trait specialization, which a lot of people focused on.
Of the 696 people who said yes, 205 included free answers. The use-cases in the free answers roughly matched these categories:
Overall, the sentiment was more cautious than in previous questions. A lot of responses to the first questions were along the lines of "Yes, I absolutely need this yesterday for X/Y/Z", whereas the responses to this question were more likely to hedge or mention hypothetical use-cases:
Not sure, maybe that can help with some not yet implemented features.
Feels like this could enhance bevy queries in some way.
This seems like a useful tool in general to work with bundles of possible behavior in a convenient and efficient way. Imagine defining systems in an ECS in terms of variadic generics that match against entities with patterns of components. Not sure exactly what this would look like, and I'd imagine it might not be possible simply through this function (might need first class types which seem overkill).
Some interesting answers:
Our company's data processing library currently uses a kludgy tuple-based method of defining data pipelines, which is constrained by max tuple length and requires a macro to define the implementation of.
VarArgs would allow us to directly have a function signature like fn pipe<...Ts>(transforms: *Ts), without the extra tuple or extra complexity
Specifically, I've wanted a variadic version of this function:
fn pipe(p1: Pipe<T1, T2>, p2: Pipe<T2, T3>, ..., pn: Pipe<Tn-1, Tn>) -> Pipe<T1, Tn>
It definitely is an 'advanced' feature, that I ultimately didn't 'need'. My use case was composable structs for building a Query, things like And<(Has<Position>, Not<Or<...>>)>, and some of these structs had creation parameters, currently a tuple is created with all parameters for structs like 'And'
But because only a subset of the structs take parameters it makes the api awkward:
And::new(((),(),...))
And I wanted to remove the unit types, I tried really hard with traits and unstable features but ultimately abandoned the idea.
Somewhat similar to how Bevy handles systems, I have built a transaction that can take in an arbitrary number of requests and execute them. Additionally, a custom logic function can be provided that takes in each request (or rather their resulting value) as an argument.
The transaction requests are in arbitrary order for API convenience, but need to be executed in a fixed order. Currently I build an array of (u8, Priority) and sort it by priority to get my order, then map the u8 values to each tuple field, execute the request and map the result onto a tuple of Option<RequestN::Result>. Finally, I return the tuple unwrapping all fields.
If I could have sorted the tuple, most of this wouldn't have been necessary.
Final questions
The second-last question was about people's priorities:
How high a priority would you say variadics are for you?
The last question was Do you have any further comments related to variadic generics?, and 572 people answered.
This last question is where skeptics who had skipped the previous questions voiced their concerns and doubts, while enthusiasts reaffirmed their support:
A lot of answers (23) were specifically about why they didn't pick "It should be the highest priority feature", and listed other features they considered more important. In those answers, "specialization" and "better const generics" were common picks.
It's hard to synthetise a coherent takeaway from all the answers at once, since a lot of them expressed incompatible wishes. The overall vibe was "cautious, but interested".
Among the skeptics, the most frequent concern was the idea that Rust might suffer a death by a thousand cuts, that an accumulation of small arcane features might make it impenetrable to new users. The skeptics were a minority, but large enough that future proposals shouldn't simply ignore them.
Future efforts to promote variadics should ideally propose a syntax that feels easy to read, and should demonstrate strong upsides over the current macro workarounds.
Finally, the last type of answer was words of encouragement from readers of the survey:
Keep up the good work!
Thank you for all the work you do!
Anyway, kudos for putting out this survey! Really appreciate the effort to surface the opinions and wishes of us amateur grug-brained type wranglers as well!
On behalf of the survey team, we'd like to return the sentiment, thank all the participants who took the time to write about their needs and concerns, and thank you for reading this far.
Also, sorry this article took so long.
The Rust community's enthusiasm is what keeps the language alive.
Thanks again!

title: Announcing the GPU notification group and Linker Working Area
text:
We are announcing two new groups in the compiler team:
- The GPU target notification group, for helping us to diagnose and resolve GPU-related issues
- The Linker working area, with expertise or interest in linkers
About the GPU-target notification group
The GPU target notification group is made of experts from various vendors (AMD, Nvidia, Intel, etc.) and its goal is to better respond to issues and in general work in this area of expertise, for example this one.
This group has an associated Zulip stream (#t-compiler/gpgpu-backend).
About the Linker working area
Creating of a linker group was discussed in MCP#964 to kickstart work about integrating alternative linkers in the compiler, like Wild. As the second goal, this group can be a point of contact for handling questions and issues regarding linkers.
This group has an associated Zulip stream (#t-compiler/linker).
What is a "notification group" and a "working area group"?
Notification groups are made of people volunteering to keep an eye and respond to issues in a specific area they have expertise, they mostly help with maintenance.
Working areas explore and do work focused on specific areas with the goal of adding features or improving the compiler.
Each group may have an associated Zulip stream where people can ask questions and discuss topics specific to that target.
Anyone can add their own name to these groups and be notified when an issue in that area is raised. If you are interested in participating, feel free to sign up for these groups. To do so, just open a PR against the rust-lang/team repository (here an example).
For more info, see the documentation about notification groups and compiler working areas.

title: Infrastructure Team 2026 Q3 Recap and Q4 Plan
text:
Here's what the Infrastructure Team delivered in Q3 2026 and what we're focusing on in Q4.
You can find the previous blog post of this series here.
Q3 2026 Accomplishments
Audit logs in Datadog Cloud SIEM
We enabled audit logs for the following services and sent them to Datadog, so that the Rust Foundation security team can analyze them using Cloud SIEM:
- The Rust GitHub Enterprise and the Rust Foundation GitHub Enterprise, via audit log streaming.
- AWS, via CloudTrail.
- Heroku, Wiz, Fastly, and Datadog itself.
See the GitHub issue for more details.
Web Application Firewall and DDoS protection for crates.io and docs.rs
Together with the crates.io and docs.rs teams, we set up the Fastly Next-Gen WAF (Web Application Firewall) for docs.rs and crates.io (see the GitHub issue). The WAF blocks potential security threats and enforces rate limits.
We also enabled Fastly DDoS protection for both services.
Together, these helped us mitigate DDoS attacks against crates.io this quarter, and reduce the load on the docs.rs server.
CDN improvements for crates.io and docs.rs
We made several improvements to the Fastly configuration of crates.io and docs.rs:
- Faster crate downloads processing: We removed a regex from the Fastly code that handles crate downloads, and did some other optimizations (#1095, #1096). Requests now take 10% less compute time in the Fastly CDN nodes. Most users won't notice the difference, since networking dominates download latency, but it makes our CDN setup more efficient and sustainable.
- Content-Length in HEAD responses: Fastly HEAD responses now include
the Content-Length header for non-compressible artifacts such as .crate files.
This fixes some issues encountered when using Buck2.
- crates.io static assets served from the edge: GET and HEAD requests for READMEs and other static
assets of crates.io are now resolved
by the CDN instead of the crates.io web app hosted on Heroku.
- docs.rs CDN logs in Datadog: The docs.rs Fastly service now sends its logs to Datadog (#1196, #1197, #1226), giving us better observability of the service.
- CloudFront traffic: In the past months, we sent 100% of crates and releases download traffic over Fastly to spend our AWS credits on other resources. We restored a small share of traffic (approximately 0.4%) over CloudFront to make sure it keeps working as intended, in case we need to fall back to it.
New message queue between crates.io and docs.rs
We provisioned an AWS SQS FIFO queue that crates.io can use to notify docs.rs about new releases.
The queue is meant to replace the crates.io git index for this use case. It's currently unused for lack of engineering time from the crates.io team.
Renovate for the rust repository
We configured Renovate
for the rust-lang/rust repository
(see the configuration file).
Renovate automatically opens PRs to fix security findings and update Cargo lockfiles and GitHub Actions.
From the dependency dashboard, maintainers can ask Renovate to update individual dependencies when they want to. You can see all the PRs opened by Renovate here.
GitHub security alerts
We enabled Dependabot alerts
in the rust-lang GitHub organization. This means that:
- Maintainers receive alerts for vulnerabilities affecting their repositories.
- Maintainers can see these vulnerabilities at https://github.com/rust-lang/<repo>/security/dependabot.
- If configured, Renovate can open PRs to fix these vulnerabilities. See the Renovate docs to learn more.
Note that this setting doesn't enable automatic Dependabot PRs. That's a separate setting called "Dependabot security updates", which we don't plan to enable because we prefer using Renovate.
More settings configured in the team repo
We keep moving manually configured settings into Infrastructure as Code (IaC) in the
team repository:
- GitHub Pages: Rust Project members can now set up GitHub Pages for their repositories by opening a PR. See the docs and an example. Thanks to cuba0001 for working on this!
- Custom Properties: GitHub Custom Properties
are now configurable in the team repo.
This allows repositories to opt in to automations developed by the Infrastructure Team.
Hardware security keys
As a follow-up to the hardware security keys work we did in Q2, we added a convention
in the team repository for Project members who want to share the PIV attestation certificates
extracted from their YubiKeys. We can validate these certificates against our inventory of hardware keys
through their serial numbers.
More details in the docs.
GitHub Actions audits
We deployed the crabwatch workflow to audit GitHub Actions
workflows in the rust-lang GitHub organization.
We enabled 23 Zizmor audits by default,
and we want to enable more in the future!
In the meantime, project members can override
what audits run in their repositories.
Thanks to Sandra, the Outreachy intern who helped us work on this! You can read about her internship experience in her blog.
Improving user experience of reviewers
Our merge queue bot (bors) is now able to gate approvals on pull request CI success in the rust-lang/rust repository.
This makes it easier for reviewers to approve pull requests without having to babysit them until PR CI succeeds.
Trusted contributors
The Rust Project created a
trusted-contributors marker team for trusted contributors who are not members of rust-lang teams but regularly contribute to rust-lang/rust.
This team has try and perf permissions, so that these contributors can start try builds and performance runs independently, without
repeatedly asking a Project member to delegate permissions.
Learn more about membership in the Forge docs.
More powerful dev desktops and Rust Playground
We upgraded the EC2 instances of the dev desktops and the Rust Playground to make these services faster for Rust contributors and the Rust community:
- Playground: from c5a.large to c7a.xlarge (PR).
- Dev desktops (PR):
  - dev-desktop-eu-1: from c6g.8xlarge to c9g.8xlarge.
  - dev-desktop-us-1: from c7g.12xlarge to c9g.12xlarge.
We also increased the disk quota to 200GB per user on all four dev desktops (#1182, #1187).
Learn more about dev desktops in the Forge docs.
ARM machine for rustc-perf
We provisioned an EC2 m9g.metal-48xl instance
to run rustc-perf on ARM.
This allows the compiler team to measure optimizations done for the ARM architecture.
New CI runners
In partnership with Canonical, we enabled new External GitHub Actions runners for the Rust Project:
- s390x-unknown-linux-gnu: currently being evaluated in the compiler-builtins repository.
- armv7-unknown-linux-gnueabihf: used in the compiler-builtins repository.
We also enabled three large ARM GitHub Actions runners (8 vCPU, 32 GB RAM) for the rustls organization, covering Ubuntu 24.04, Ubuntu 26.04, and Windows 11. This additional CI capacity is sponsored by ARM.
riscv64gc-unknown-linux-musl promoted to tier 2 with host tools
We promoted the riscv64gc-unknown-linux-musl target
to tier 2 with host tools.
RISC-V users targeting musl no longer need to compile Rust tools like rustc and cargo themselves.
On-call rotation moved to Datadog
Since the Rust Foundation joined Datadog's Open Source Program, we migrated the Rust Foundation on-call rotation from PagerDuty to Datadog On-Call. This allows us to save money and to remove one service from our dependencies.
Team leader rotation
We established a new policy for the Infrastructure Team leader.
As a result, we rotated one team leader: Marco took the place of JD.
Main branch
We renamed the default branch of 25 repositories to main: lang-team, rustc-hash, rustc-perf, rust-artwork, .github, compiler-team-prioritization, project-ffi-unwind, project-safe-transmute, wg-allocators, wg-cargo-std-aware, futures-rs, pin-utils, thanks, rust-forge, triagebot, mdBook, portable-simd, rustup-components-history, std-dev-guide, polonius, cargo-bisect-rustc, rust-mode, rust.vim, types-team, rfcs.
Among public repositories in the rust-lang organization that are neither archived nor forks,
113 use main and 56 still use master.
Trusted publishing
We converted 7 crates to use trusted publishing:
Triagebot Assign-priority command
We improved and added a shortcut to the assign-priority command (e747558e), see docs on the forge.
Q4 2026 Plans
Finish Q3 goals
In Q3, we didn't manage to finish all our goals, so we will continue working on them in Q4:
- Improve access controls for Rust infrastructure with SAML SSO.
- Move mailing lists from Mailgun to Google Groups to reduce spam.
- Consolidate logs on Datadog.
- Stricter networking access rules for crater agents.
You can read more about these goals in our Q3 2026 plan.
Secure deployments
Today, we deploy infrastructure from our personal laptops. Instead, we want to deploy from a secure environment with strong access controls, where access is limited to the people who maintain the deployment processes. Deploying from a centralized environment also makes it easier to automate deployments and to monitor for unauthorized access or suspicious activity.
As a first step, we want to simplify our Infrastructure as Code setup, which currently uses both Terraform and Terragrunt. We want to investigate whether it is still worth using both tools (see the GitHub issue).
After simplifying the setup, we will decide how to automate deployments and start automating them.
Decommission the monitoring instance
As part of our move to Datadog, we want to decommission our self-hosted monitoring instance, which runs Prometheus, Alertmanager and Grafana.
Join us
If you're interested in contributing to Rust's infrastructure, have a look at the infra-team repository to learn more about us and reach out on Zulip.
We are always looking for new contributors!
